maintopic: FURTHER STATEMENT ON FOREST ACCESS ROADS TO PROVIDE WINTER EMPLOYMENT

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

speakeroldname: Hon. Alvin Hamilton (Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources):
speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
maintopic: FURTHER STATEMENT ON FOREST ACCESS ROADS TO PROVIDE WINTER EMPLOYMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, when I made a statement in the house yesterday, as recorded at page 2774 of Hansard of that date, the hon. member for Montmagny-L'lslet asked the following supplementary question:
Is the signature on that agreement-
Meaning an agreement on forest fire protection signed pursuant to the Canada Forestry Act.
-a condition of the obtaining of a part of those funds for access roads for forest fire protection?
I answered this question in the affirmative, but on reading Hansard I realize that the words "those funds" used by my hon. friend did not refer to funds under the forest fire protection agreements but to the new funds to be requested of parliament for forestry access roads; hence my subsequent reply to the hon. member's question may have been misleading.
It is clear, of course, that in order to obtain funds provided by parliament for the implementation of the forest Are protection agreements a province must have concluded such an agreement with the federal government.
It is equally clear that in order to get federal aid for the construction of forestry access roads under an agreement to cover the period of January 2 to June 30, 1958, a province must conclude an agreement with the federal government and funds must be provided by parliament. But it is not necessary for any province to participate in both agreements before deriving benefits under one agreement.
Naturally, some adjustments must be made with regard to provinces which participate in both agreements. The reason for this is that under the forest fire protection agreement the federal contribution for access roads is limited to 25 per cent. Under the short winter program, proposed especially for access roads, regardless of their purpose, be it for fire protection or for forest management, the contribution offered for this short period is 50 per cent. After June 30, 1958, those provinces which have signed the forest fire protection agreements can claim only 25 per cent.
As Quebec is the only province which has not concluded a forest fire protection agreement, Mr. Speaker, if it concludes an agreement on access roads valid until June 30,

1958, it cannot claim thereafter a 25 per cent contribution by virtue of another agreement which it has not signed. Both agreements are open to all provinces independently on an equal footing.
In a very clear story this morning in the Globe and Mail this winter works program is described accurately and fully. However, in one paragraph there is a misunderstanding which is probably my responsibility. This paragraph says:
Quebec-the only one of ten provinces which has not signed a federal-provincial agreement on forest fire protection-will not be able to participate in the road project.
Therefore I would like to stress again that Quebec can participate in this new program without signing the forest fire protection agreement. To make this absolutely clear, and since there were small changes in the letter to Premier Duplessis in order to take account of the fact that Quebec has not signed a forest fire protection agreement, it might be useful, if the house agreed, for me to table this letter to Premier Duplessis in the original French and in the English version in order that it may be printed as an appendix to Hansard.

maintopic: FURTHER STATEMENT ON FOREST ACCESS ROADS TO PROVIDE WINTER EMPLOYMENT

speechtext:

maintopic: FURTHER STATEMENT ON FOREST ACCESS ROADS TO PROVIDE WINTER EMPLOYMENT
speechtext: May I ask the minister whether it will be a condition of the 50 per cent participation by the government in the building of those access roads-I am talking about the winter program-that tenders be asked by the provinces for those works?

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
maintopic: FURTHER STATEMENT ON FOREST ACCESS ROADS TO PROVIDE WINTER EMPLOYMENT
speechtext: I will have to look at the letter. My memory is that there is no such condition asked of any of the provinces in the letter.

maintopic: FURTHER STATEMENT ON FOREST ACCESS ROADS TO PROVIDE WINTER EMPLOYMENT
speechtext: May I ask a supplementary question and preface it by saying that in the forest fire protection agreements there is a condition that tenders have to be called. Would not the same condition be in the agreements which will be signed for this short winter program?

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
maintopic: FURTHER STATEMENT ON FOREST ACCESS ROADS TO PROVIDE WINTER EMPLOYMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I thought the hon. member would realize that in making these announcements of
Inquiries of the Ministry policy you do not go into all the details. There will have to be an agreement drawn with each of the provinces, and I certainly think this question of tenders will be considered as part of the agreement.

maintopic: FURTHER STATEMENT ON FOREST ACCESS ROADS TO PROVIDE WINTER EMPLOYMENT
speechtext: I should like to ask a supplementary question of the minister. Has he given any consideration to the possibility that making the terminal date of these agreements June 30 may be rather limiting it, on account of weather, in the Atlantic provinces and particularly in Newfoundland. If we should have a backward spring in 1958, such as we had in 1957, it would be physically impossible to get this work done by June 30. Would he consider the possibility, in those cases where weather would be a factor, of having the date somewhat later?

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
maintopic: FURTHER STATEMENT ON FOREST ACCESS ROADS TO PROVIDE WINTER EMPLOYMENT
speechtext:
Yes, Mr. Speaker. This matter was very carefully considered by the forestry branch of my department, and in some other works projects which we are announcing winter employment will end on May 31. For instance, in some that have already been announced employment will end sooner than that. But on this question of forestry access roads we recognize the necessity of being able to do the grading in the summer months. Therefore in deciding on June 30 we took that into consideration. In the first few months the clearing which can be done during the winter would be done to provide employment. Following the break-up period we would have the two months of May and June to do the grading, which would consummate the program.
In regard to the province of Newfoundland I will ask the officials to look into that point again, to make certain there is no hardship in completing the program in that province.

maintopic: FURTHER STATEMENT ON FOREST ACCESS ROADS TO PROVIDE WINTER EMPLOYMENT
speechtext: I appreciate the minister's attitude very much.

maintopic: FURTHER STATEMENT ON FOREST ACCESS ROADS TO PROVIDE WINTER EMPLOYMENT

maintopic: FURTHER STATEMENT ON FOREST ACCESS ROADS TO PROVIDE WINTER EMPLOYMENT

Under the
criteria I have announced I think this road might be considered as part of this program, but actually the province of Saskatchewan has made representations to the government on different grounds with respect to the road. These representations are now being considered, and at this time I would rather that this matter be kept separate until we reach

Inquiries of the Ministry some final conclusion with the province of Saskatchewan with regard to the Hanson lake road.

subtopic: REQUEST FOR STATEMENT ON RECENT DISCUSSIONS

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

subtopic: REQUEST FOR STATEMENT ON RECENT DISCUSSIONS
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, before the Minister of Finance went abroad he told us he anticipated having discussions with United Kingdom ministers about the forthcoming commonwealth trade conference. Can he bring us up to date with regard to these discussions?

speakeroldname: Hon. Donald M. Fleming (Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: REQUEST FOR STATEMENT ON RECENT DISCUSSIONS
speechtext:
Yes, Mr. Speaker, I shall be glad to do so. While in London I had a meeting with the chancellor of the exchequer, the president of the board of trade and their officials two weeks ago yesterday, December 20. In discussing this question we had the opportunity of reviewing the whole situation. The British government proposes to send out invitations to all the commonwealth governments to send their officials to London early in February for a meeting to make plans at the official level.
It is expected that there will be two stages to the official preparations for the conference. There will be this meeting of officials in February, and it is likely there will be a further meeting of officials in the spring at which detailed work will be done on the items to come before the conference.
The date of the conference has not yet been finally determined. There is some difference of view among some of the countries of the commonwealth as to which dates would suit their governments best; there have been changes of governments in two of the commonwealth countries. It is our hope, however, that the date and place of the conference can be decided soon.

subtopic: REQUEST FOR STATEMENT ON RECENT DISCUSSIONS
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, may I ask a supplementary question. Did the minister make any progress during these talks in discussing the proposals which Mr. Thorneycroft made when he was here in September?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: REQUEST FOR STATEMENT ON RECENT DISCUSSIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, that subject was not mentioned. Our concern and purpose were to make plans for the commonwealth trade and economic conference. The situation is precisely as it was reported to this house and to the public in the statement which was issued here in Ottawa following the meeting of the ministers of the United Kingdom government and ministers of the Canadian government in the first week of October of last year.


The governments of the commonwealth countries are concentrating on the plans for the commonwealth trade and economic conference and wish to make a thorough success of it, and any commonwealth country which wishes to bring forward any proposals in relation to trade within the commonwealth, or to economic questions arising within the commonwealth, or economic policies, will have full opportunity of putting them before the trade and economic conference.

subtopic: REQUEST FOR STATEMENT ON RECENT DISCUSSIONS
speechtext: I wonder if the minister could give us any idea of the kind of proposals Canada intends to put forward at this conference. It is surely not going to be held in vacuo?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: REQUEST FOR STATEMENT ON RECENT DISCUSSIONS
speechtext: I think the hon. gentleman will realize on reflection that his question is quite premature.

subtopic: REQUEST FOR STATEMENT ON RECENT DISCUSSIONS
speechtext: further supplementary question, Mr. Speaker. Is it not a fact that the preparations for this conference are now in the hands of the British and not the Canadian government?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: REQUEST FOR STATEMENT ON RECENT DISCUSSIONS
speechtext: No, the hon. gentleman is quite wrong. I think it is very likely that agreement will be reached to hold this conference in Canada, but it was considered by practically all the commonwealth ministers represented at Mont Tremblant-and the statements made there have been confirmed since-that London would be the most convenient place for holding the conferences of officials in preparation for the plenary conference. Consequently, in these circumstances, the British government offered to be host in London to the meetings of the officials. It is a matter for general arrangement, but I think I am warranted in saying that the invitation of the Canadian government to hold the plenary conference in Canada will be accepted by all countries.

speechtext: When the committee rose last evening it was considering the details of item No. 240 under the various headings set out on pages 313 to 315. Discussion was proceeding on the items under the heading "Canadian army, regular and general" on pages 326 to 334. Has discussion under this heading been concluded?

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
No, Mr. Chairman, it had not been concluded at ten o'clock last evening. I would like to ask permission of the Chair to raise a matter which I raised last evening but the answer to which I did not think was satisfactory. I am glad the Minister of Transport is here, because he is concerned with the matter as well.
Last evening I asked the Minister of National Defence what the position was with regard to the H.M.C.S. Labrador. As I said
Supply-National Defence earlier I thought the answer was certainly lacking in information; and I say this respectfully to him, of course. What I have difficulty in understanding is this. The Department of National Defence had an icebreaker built for its own purposes at a substantial cost. My information is that it cost in the neighbourhood of some $25 million. The cost of an icebreaker for peacetime purposes is less than half that amount.
An icebreaker built for naval purposes is a vessel of an entirely different nature and equipment than that of a Department of Transport icebreaking vessel; and why H.M. C.S. Labrador would be assigned to a peacetime department when it was built for a different purpose is something that I think should be explained to the house more thoroughly than was done last night. In other words, I think the minister should tell us why it is that the Department of National Defence, which required this icebreaker for a definite purpose, now says it is no longer necessary for that purpose. There must be a reason for the change.
The other thing which I think should be explained to the house is why this vessel which was built for a specific purpose is no longer being used for that purpose but is being turned over to a peacetime department exclusively for icebreaking purposes. I hope the minister will come to the conclusion that I am seeking information. I think the committee is entitled to an explanation as to why this has been done.

Mr. Chairman, reverting
to the item under the heading "Navy" under which the hon. gentleman raised his question, my understanding is that the Labrador was built as an icebreaker and that there was very little difference in the construction of the Labrador from that of the ordinary icebreaker. It was of rather heavier construction for the more northern waters, and will be available for that work under the Department of Transport if work of that nature is again required. She carried out certain exploratory work which was more of a civilian nature than technically a naval matter. After careful consideration and following consultation with the officials of the Department of Transport, we felt that the Labrador could be used to better advantage under the Department of Transport than under the Department of National Defence.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
Well, Mr. Chairman, I do not have these officials at my disposal who know, I am sure, far more about the position than I do; but I have been aboard both the Labrador and the C. D. Howe, the two most up to date icebreakers of the Department of

Supply-National Defence Transport, and I say to the minister in deference that they are like night and day as to the equipment that is on board each. The proof of that lies in the cost. Surely an icebreaker which costs in the neighbourhood of $25 million must have something in it that is far superior to one that cost $5 million or $6 million; and comparing their value and cost my impression is that one must have been built for a specific purpose, namely the purpose of defence in the Arctic waters as well as icebreaking, of course, which was incidental, and the Department of Transport icebreaker which is entirely a peacetime vessel. However, I do not intend to pursue it unnecessarily and unduly, though I say with respect that I am not satisfied with the answer I have received.

Mr. Chairman, I should like to follow up what the hon. member for Laurier has said. I am rather concerned about the Labrador being transferred from the navy to the Department of Transport. I understood when this ship was built that the navy required the ship for Arctic work. The minister said she would be available, of course, in case of necessity. What does this mean? It means that if hostilities broke out she would be transferred back to the navy. Has the minister any figures on the actual operating cost of the Labrador by the navy? What is it going to cost now to refit this ship for the Department of Transport?

Mr. Chairman, since we passed this naval item yesterday I have not the naval advisers here, so I cannot possibly give an answer to that question; but I can obtain it and let the hon. member have it at the beginning of the week.

Has the army area headquarters located in Fredericton been transferred to any other location?
No; the area headquarters is at Fredericton.

There are one or two questions in my mind emanating from the communique of the NATO powers in Paris. Perhaps the minister would care to explain this statement:
As regards defence production, we have decided, in view of the progress already made, to take further measures within NATO to promote the co-ordination of research, development and manufacture of modern weapons including intermediate range ballistic missiles.
Will the minister please tell us what is being done to promote this co-ordination in these fields of research and development and in the manufacture of weapons? What is actually being done?

That question could better be put when we come to the item for the defence research board, but there is co-ordination going on. There have been a number of exchanges of visits between senior officials of the United States forces and of the British forces. As the hon. gentleman knows, there were set up at the NATO conference certain advisers on the scientific and research staff, and it is hoped that there will be frequent

and regular consultations among the representatives of all NATO countries on the matter of research and development.
Can the minister outline, perhaps briefly, what plans his department has for improving the property known as Camp	Chippewa during	1958?

Did the	hon.	gentleman	say
"Camp Chippewa"?
Yes.

plans for any changes in that camp.
Do I understand that there will be no improvement in that property in this calendar year?

There	are	no	plans	for
extensive improvement. The ordinary maintenance will be kept up.
In other words it is intended to drop the plans that were scheduled for improving the property?
I am advised that there are no special plans for any further construction at Chippewa. The ordinary maintenance will be kept up, but no expansion is planned for that camp.

Since the minister has informed me that the army area headquarters have not been moved from Fredericton, can he explain why army camps in other areas a long distance from Gagetown have been closed? I am informed that the camp at Fredericton has a very high maintenance cost. It is located in a very beautiful part of the city which perhaps could be used to much better advantage. Those working at the army area headquarters in Fredericton would be inconvenienced very little by a move of 12 or 14 miles to Gagetown.
Can the minister explain why a camp such as Camp Utopia in Charlotte county would be closed and a camp in the city of Fredericton would be maintained? I have been asked this question by many people, and I can assure the minister that there is a great interest in the province of New Brunswick concerning this matter as it is felt that army headquarters in Fredericton could have been moved and the Utopia camp maintained at very little cost to the government.

As the hon. member knows. Camp Gagetown has been under construction for a number of years. The intention was that the training of all the units in the Atlantic provinces would take place at Gagetown, and that the regular army units would be stationed there as soon as the accommodation was completed.

The hon. member asked me whether the headquarters were still at Fredericton. My answer was that the headquarters are still at Fredericton. There is no camp at Fredericton, but at the present moment there is no spare accommodation at Gagetown. Units are moving into Gagetown as soon as accommodation is made available. It is under consideration whether at some future date, when the accommodation question is adjusted, the headquarters for that area might not be moved from Fredericton to Gagetown, but the accommodation is not available at the present time.
Did the minister say there were no personnel at army headquarters in Fredericton? Did he say that the personnel there had been moved?
I said there was no camp at Fredericton, but the headquarters are still retained in the administration building there.

Mr. Chairman, the answer the minister gave to my last question was completely unsatisfactory and thoroughly disheartening. The only reason I excuse him is that, as he said and probably legitimately so, he was not dealing with his own department and this was really a matter for defence production. Nevertheless, when the Minister of National Defence tells me that the degree of co-ordination we have achieved after all these years is limited to the exchange of visits, the setting up of a group of advisers and frequent consultations, I should like to know what is the meaning of the word "co-ordination". However, I will ask him another question which I think he possibly can answer in view of the fact that we have in Europe a brigade and an air division. This arises again out of this awful communique from Paris.
Recognizing the rapidly growing interdependence of the nations of the free world-
These cliches are not mine, Mr. Chairman.
-we have, in organizing our forces, decided to bring about closer co-ordination with a view to ensuring that each NATO member country makes its most effective contribution . . .
Will the minister please translate those words into something tangible? Will he tell us what is actually happening in the way of co-ordination of the armed forces of NATO?

Co-ordination of the armed forces of NATO will be discussed in detail when the meeting of the defence ministers of the NATO countries takes place next March. The communique to which the hon. member refers was really an outline of the principles agreed upon by the heads of states. The details will have to be worked

Supply-National Defence out at the subsequent meeting which, as I have said, has been called for early in the year, March or April, I believe.
There is one point on which the hon. member misunderstood my remarks. I did not say that this was a matter for defence production. I referred to the defence research board, which is a later item in this estimate.

Am I to
accept the minister's statement that despite the many speeches that have been made by ministers since NATO was founded, we are only going to start to co-ordinate our forces this year? Has there been no attempt at coordination in the past, or have we been deceived throughout all these years by these vague and pious statements emanating from men whose minds are still in the Maginot era?

That is a most ridiculous statement. Long before the present government came into power meetings were held. Ever since the NATO organization was established there have been meetings of the defence ministers every year, and there is a very high measure of co-ordination now among the NATO countries. That co-ordination will continue, and the next meeting of the defence ministers is in March.

In that case why is this particular paragraph included in the communique? Second, when I asked for some information about co-ordination why did the minister tell me that this would be decided at the next meeting of defence ministers? On that basis one can assume legitimately that nothing much had been done about it before. What I want to know is not about the next meeting of ministers and the hopes that may be raised as a result of that meeting, but what has actually happened in the field of co-ordination up to the present. How efficiently co-ordinated are the forces or, indeed, is there co-ordination in any sense of the word?

Unfortunately I was not here yesterday, but I noticed in Hansard that there was an exchange between the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre and the minister with regard to the apparent conflict between statements made by the minister before the NATO conference and statements made by the Prime Minister after the conference, in that the minister had indicated earlier that it was the hope of the government to be able to curtail and economize on defence expenditures and the Prime Minister indicated that colossal further spending would be necessary.
I quite understand the logic of the minister's suggestion that he cannot discuss next


year's estimates while we are still discussing the current estimates, but I would suggest that the defence expenditures we are making today cannot be considered in a vacuum and as purely concerned with the year that ends on March 31, 1958. Surely they must have some relationship to future plans of the government with regard to defence spending.
Therefore I think we are entitled to at least some indication from the minister with respect to whether or not the government is still of the mind which he expressed earlier, that it will be possible to reduce the colossal spendings that are going on at the present time; or do we have to contemplate even greater ones as suggested by the Prime Minister? It seems to me that the government should tell us quite frankly whether or not they are still of the opinion that in the present circumstances the type of defence spending that has been going on in Canada is really of any relevance in the world of modern warfare.

All these expenditures have been very carefully considered, and we believe that the amount of money allocated for defence as reflected in these estimates is very definitely related to the commitments we have to make both for the defence of this country and our obligations under our NATO and United Nations commitments. It is impossible at this time to give any indication as to the extent of next year's estimates.

Can the minister inform the house whether, as a result of the annual review of the NATO authorities which must have been discussed at the last council meeting, any requests were made of the Canadian government which would require any modification of our military contribution to NATO?

As the hon. member knows, there is an annual review which is submitted to the different countries and which will be discussed at the March meeting. My recollection is that no substantial change in the size of the forces Canada is contributing has been recommended.

I understand that in addition to the annual review which is part of NATO's normal procedure a reassessment of NATO's military planning, tactics and strategy has been made or is being made by the NATO military authorities. Can the minister say whether or not that reassessment has been completed, or whether it remains to be discussed at the March meeting to which he has referred?

That remains to be discussed at the March meeting. Our commitments are

constantly under review. Certain recommendations have been made by the commander, General Norstad, and those are receiving consideration of the department now.
Will the minister tell the committee if his department has considered the offer of the city of St. Jerome to buy the drill hall in that city, which has not been in use for quite a long time?
I shall have to check that. If the hon. member would not mind, I will get the information later this day.

I have visited the Canadian brigade camp in Germany since I became Minister of National Defence. I paid a short visit to the camp again in July of this year.

Supply-[DOT]National Defence I can support the statements I made previously that the buildings and camps are of a very high order. Our troops are well accommodated in Germany, and I think it is necessary that they should be well accommodated in order that their morale may be retained. It is not an easy task for any troops to be stationed in a foreign country, surrounded by people who speak a different language and who, while friendly, cannot be entirely intimate; the same relationship cannot exist as if those troops were stationed in their own land.
Certain amenities have to be provided, as I indicated in the remarks the hon. member read, in the way of providing special food, special schools and that sort of thing. Those are being maintained and will be maintained as long as we keep troops in western Europe. We have a commitment with NATO that we will maintain one brigade group in Europe. Until we are relieved of that commitment I do not believe Canada would think of making a unilateral decision to withdraw those troops. In fact, I believe it is essential for the preservation of peace and for the maintenance of that unity which was shown at this last NATO meeting among all NATO countries, that we have a contingent in Europe for the time being.
It is to be hoped that when the forces of West Germany are reorganized and their training has been completed, and they have in existence the number of troops contemplated, there may then be an opportunity of reducing our commitment in Europe. I will admit it is a heavy drain on the economy, but it is an international agreement which we have made. Until it is agreed by our allies that our forces should be withdrawn, I do not see how we can make any material reduction in those forces.

Two years ago I think the fact that the minister referred to the flying of pasteurized milk to Germany implied that he thought, in view of the importance of the dairy industry in that part of the world, that was a type of economy that might be contemplated. Can the minister indicate whether any change has been made? Is milk still being flown from Canada to Germany? I gather that was the criticism he intended to make two years ago when he raised the question.
Milk is at present being obtained from Denmark under contract.

The minister has talked about our NATO commitment, and has said that it would be inappropriate to modify that commitment without the approval of our fellow members of NATO. As he knows, of course,


that commitment we share with other NATO members. Perhaps it is worth putting on the record that certain other members of NATO-and I am not criticizing them for this-by unilateral action have already modified their commitments in that regard.
I do not think the hon. member is suggesting that Canada should make a unilateral change, is he?

No, I am not; but I do not think we should take on commitments of a different kind or of a different nature than those which are undertaken by the other members of NATO. We are all in exactly the same position. Inasmuch as other members of NATO, for reasons which may be very good both for them and for NATO, have by their own decision found it necessary to modify their commitments, I just question the minister's categorical statement that it would be impossible or inappropriate for us to alter our commitment in any regard except after agreement with all the NATO members. I think that statement just should be put on the record.
I think it would be inappropriate for Canada to change her commitment without discussing it with her allies.
Discussion is one thing; agreement is another.

I was greatly disappointed to hear the Minister of National Defence say that he knew of no plans for improving the property known as the Camp Chippewa site at North Bay during 1958. Perhaps he is not aware of the fact that his department acquired this property from the city of North Bay on the distinct understanding that they would improve it. I certainly know the people of North Bay will be greatly disappointed to learn that the new government does not intend to go ahead with that proposal or with that definite, firm understanding. I wonder whether the minister would look into this matter and attempt to give me some kind of satisfactory answer.

I will look into that detail and let the hon. member know; but as far as I know at the present time there is no intention of extending that project. However, I will check on the matter, make certain and let the hon. member know this afternoon.

Perhaps I might explain that when they acquired the property from the city there was a firm undertaking by his department that they would improve and clean up that area. We are building a beautiful new high school directly across the street and there is substantial housing

in that area. There must be improvement in that property. I certainly hope it will be proceeded with.
I will look into the matter and let the hon. member know this afternoon.

I wonder whether the minister can give us any sort of rough estimate as to what proportion of our total defence spending is involved in our NATO commitments. I realize it will be difficult to do, but perhaps we might be able to get some idea of how much is involved in the NATO commitments.

In round figures the cost of maintaining the air division in Europe is $90 million and the cost of maintaining the brigade is $30 million. That refers to that portion of our NATO commitments which is in Europe. Of course we have our commitments as far as NATO is concerned in connection with the navy and in connection with the air force in the defence of this North American continent, all of which are part of the general scheme for the prevention of war.
By the minister's answer am I to understand that all Canada's defence spendings are in effect NATO commitments either in North America or in Europe?

Our whole defence policy is based on the deterrent against and the prevention of war, linked up with our NATO allies. We are not operating as a single country trying to provide for the defence of Canada. Our whole defence policy is related to the general NATO policy for the prevention of war.

The minister has mentioned the portion of our defence policy which he referred to as the deterrent power. Can he tell us whether the Canadian government has at its disposal any weapon or deterrent power for the protection of North America?
No, Mr. Chairman. "Deterrent", did the hon. member say?
Yes.
Yes, certainly. I think all our forces contribute in some measure or another to the deterrent against war.
Are there deterrents against guided missiles? Have we any deterrent against those?

We have no direct defence against the guided missile at the present time; that is as to a missile launched,-if it was possible, from some foreign country against this continent. There would be no direct defence against that. I do not think any direct defence exists at the present time. If the hon.
Supply-National Defence member is thinking of the possibility of guided missiles being launched from ships at sea, of course we have a deterrent in our navy which would keep the launching ship, we hope, far away from our shores.

The minister was speaking of defence, and he was speaking earlier of deterrent power which I have always understood to be the power to pursue a policy of what Mr. Dulles called massive retaliation in order to prevent an attack rather than defend against it. Have we in our possession or is there in the government's possession any method of deterrent in that form? Is it possible for us to deter a missile attack against Canadian territory?

The power of retaliation is in the main based with the strategic air force of the United States and with the bomber forces and the rocket forces now being developed in the United Kingdom and in western Europe. We have no part in that phase of the deterrent, namely the power of retaliation.

Then do I take it, Mr. Chairman, that Canada is not able to play any part in the defence which is dependent on the power of retaliation to deter attacks: that we are dependent entirely on the United States and Britain. Is that correct?

Canada is a member of the NATO organization. We have tried to coordinate and assign to the different countries the part they are best able to play in the whole defence scheme. We have a very important part to play as far as the defence of this North American continent is concerned. We have not taken on any part with regard to the forces of retaliation other than to provide protection for those forces of retaliation by our warning system, our air defence command here on the North American continent, and naval patrols which would prevent enemy submarines from interfering with the powers of retaliation. Also there is our contribution in Europe, which acts as a shield and protection to the forces which are established in Europe and which can take part in measures of retaliation.

Well, Mr. Chairman, I
understood the minister to say that the power of deterrent by means of possible retaliation lies with the strategic air command. That does not agree with his statement that our contribution to NATO is a contribution to power, because the strategic air command is not, I understand, under the command of NATO at all but entirely under the command of the United States administration. Is that not true?

Supply-National Defence

The deterrent must be viewed as a whole. It is in two parts. One is the defensive measures which protect the powers of retaliation and prevent the possibility of the enemy gaining successes, and the second is the power of retaliation. The launching of that retaliation is, as I think the hon. member said, a matter for decision by the President of the United States.

And can the minister tell us in view of that fact-it would be a matter of interest to Canadians-if the United States has at its command the necessary weapons now to produce massive retaliation in the event of a guided missile attack?

From the information which I received at NATO I am convinced that NATO is strong today.
As to the details regarding United States plans for retaliation, that is another country and it is not for me to answer or to give details regarding that matter.

But I must remind the minister that he has already told us in effect that we rely on the United States strategic air command for the power of retaliation as an instrument in our defence, and I do not think he can very well slide back into NATO again when he has told us that. I think it is of importance to us to know whether the strategic air command of the United States upon which we apparently rely is now in possession of weapons able to supply that protection.
I am confident that the United States and other NATO countries have a power of retaliation which will be very effective.

On the point we have been discussing, Mr. Chairman, the committee will of course be aware that a great deal of detailed information on this very matter has recently been given during congressional investigations in Washington by Americans in charge of national defence. The information is all on the record there now, so there is nothing very secret about it.
I want to ask the minister whether he has any comment to make on a story which appeared in the London Free Press of December 27, and which is reported to have been based on information supplied by the directorate of public relations for the army in Ottawa. The nature of the story will be indicated by the first paragraph of this report, which I will read. It is as follows:
Second battalion, the Royal Canadian regiment, now in Wolseley barracks, (London), has been placed on constant stand-by alert to move into any


trouble spot in the world if necessary, as Canada's contribution to a United Nations or NATO emergency force, it was learned today.

After the experience which was acquired when there came a demand to send a Canadian unit to Suez, the decision was reached to have one stand-by battalion ready for any emergency, not earmarked necessarily for the United Nations, but for any emergency.
I can give an example of the changes which are brought about by that decision. In a good many of the units-and this applied particularly when the Queen's Own was ordered to go to Suez-it was found that there were a number of men who were under the age when it was desirable that men should leave this country on active service. By earmarking one battalion for immediate readiness we have eliminated the younger men from that battalion and created a unit which would be ready for any emergency which might occur.

Mr. Chairman, the minister has made striking changes in the militia- I notice this matter may be discussed under a subheading the details of which we are now discussing-but in spite of the statements the minister has made I am convinced there is still a great deal of doubt in the minds of members of the militia as to when their units might lose their identity.
The minister has explained about the various columns into which the militia would be divided for civil defence purposes, but I still find there is doubt in the minds of the people of Canada as to which body would be replacing the militia in case of infiltration by enemy troops or the infiltration of agents into certain districts. Considering also the fact that the military training given to militia units is now greatly reduced compared with what it formerly was, I wonder if the minister would make a statement bringing us up to date on the militia today, and whether he would also give us a forecast as to future unit recognition, telling us what body he thinks would replace the militia in the event, for instance, of local skirmishes in the absence of the permanent forces.

There is no force contemplated to take the place of the militia. The militia has a very important role to play in the general defence program. Emphasis is being placed this year on the ability of the militia to play its part in aid of the civil power if a disaster should occur here in Canada. They are being trained especially this year in order to maintain the ability of this nation to survive if this country should come under attack. It is a realistic role, and

one which can be allocated to a force which is composed of citizen soldiers many of whom are closely in touch with the civil authorities by the very nature of their civilian employment.
This does not mean they are not to continue their training in the other roles in which they might possibly be employed. All the advice I received from the best military judgment indicates that if there is another major war it will start with a period of intense nuclear activity, and this continent and this country might well be a target for hostile bombers or even for missiles if our deterrent fails. In order to be able to play their part in those preliminary phases of another war the militia are concentrating on their role in aid to the civilian power, and it is being organized so that each militia unit will be able to make a definite contribution in that regard.

Mr. Chairman, I notice
that on three occasions the minister was at pains to lay emphasis on the statement that the training was for this year. I was wondering if he could forecast if this civil defence training was merely for this year, and if he was going to revert next year to the training the militia previously had?

No. The militia will always, as far as I can see, have a very definite role to play in the first battle for survival in this country, and we will continue to emphasize the importance of that; but we will not overlook other possible future roles, and so the know-how of the ordinary military training will have to be maintained. I must emphasize the fact that I believe military training, disciplined troops, would have a tremendous effect in restoring order in an area which had been under attack or which had met with some catastrophe. The appearance of an organized, disciplined, uniformed body would do more to restore morale than almost anything else. Therefore we must concentrate part of the militia's training toward the relief of such a catastrophe on the importance of discipline and military training as such.

Mr. Chairman, I should like to say that when I had the responsibility for civil defence I always found my hon. friend very objective and responsible with regard to the very difficult problem involved in trying to provide for the defence of the civilian population against modern potential warfare. While I realize that civil defence does not come under the purview of the Minister of National Defence, the responsibility of the two departments in this particular is so related that I do not think it inappropriate to ask the Minister of National Defence one or two questions having to do
Supply-National Defence directly with civil defence. I would hope certainly that before the conclusion of this session we could anticipate some statement by the responsible minister, the Minister of National Health and Welfare, with respect to this difficult question of civil defence.
The suggestion has been made, of course, that the only effective way of providing for civil defence is through the use of mobile columns provided largely from the militia itself. This view is predicated upon an alleged practice that has been embarked upon in the United Kingdom. As I am sure my hon. friend knows, the extent of the use of these mobile columns in the United Kingdom has been greatly exaggerated. I think it would be well, if the minister feels that is the case, if he would indicate this; because there are many thousands of people in Canada interested in civil defence who are somewhat frustrated and who are influenced to some degree by the suggestion that the proper way to provide for civil defence is through the use of the militia.
I think it is a well known fact that it had been rather well established at least a year before the previous government vacated office that the militia, the reserve forces and the armed forces generally would be indoctrinated to a much greater extent than heretofore in the matter of civil defence. It would be useful for the minister to indicate what increased use is being made by the armed forces, for instance, of the civil defence college, of the training received there; what additional civil defence training is afforded the armed forces at the Royal Military College or elsewhere, to indicate an increasing realization by the armed forces of the responsibility for civil defence and the part the armed forces can play in this very difficult matter.
It might also be useful for the minister to indicate his views, if he is now in a position to do so-and I am not pressing him because I know the difficulty-about the practicality of evacuation as a defence against atomic and thermonuclear warfare. He might indicate, too, what is the view of the Department of National Defence with regard to civil defence in so far as it has to do with the intercontinental ballistic missile, and what is the latest thinking.
I raise these questions not in a critical way, because this is too important a matter to raise for the purpose of political embarrassment. This is an extremely difficult problem, and I know it perhaps as well as anyone in this house. It seems to me that the government does have a direct responsibility if we are spending these huge sums of money for the maintenance of our freedom



Supply-National Defence and integrity-and I see no alternative to our so doing-as an insurance premium, as the leader of the opposition often used to say about the cost of NATO. By the same process of reasoning it must be presumed that the civilian population of the country must be afforded some measure of defence against the terrible potential that could exist in modern warfare.
Does the minister think that the basic lines of civilian defence pursued in this country by the provinces, the federal government and the municipalities, relying upon the municipalities, relying upon the municipality as the main arm with the co-ordinated effort of government is the right course? If it is not, do my hon. friends have some changes in mind? Perhaps this would be the appropriate moment for the Minister of National Defence to give us the benefit of his thinking and of his assessment since he became the minister responsible for national defence.

I have always emphasized the fact that the role which the militia is to play in civil defence is that of aid to the civil power. I take exception to the remark -perhaps it was not intentional-made by the hon. member that mobile columns were the only form of defence.
In the United Kingdom. I was referring to the United Kingdom.

I think the situation is quite different here owing to the distance between cities. I can see a great value in having an organized body of militiamen capable of moving into an adjacent area which has been destroyed by enemy action or by some act of God. We are organizing those columns, of which there will be approximately 50 distributed across the country, consisting of reconnaissance companies, rescue companies, communications companies, traffic control companies and that sort of thing. Each militia unit will be given a definite quota of subunits ready to move into any adjacent area which has had the misfortune of being attacked or, if there are any survivors after an attack in their own particular area, to be there to give aid.
But there is no basic change in the concept of the role of the militia to aid the civil power. I want to emphasize that point. The militia is not taking over civil defence. The responsibility for civil defence still rests with the provinces and the municipalities. I am sure the Minister of National Health and Welfare will support that contention when he speaks.
We are stepping up the training of the militia and the regular army in their duties

in connection with civil defence, and we are increasing the attendance at courses at the Arnprior civil defence college. There is to be a staff course conducted there, a sort of staff study, between the senior militia officers and the senior officials of civil defence in order to ensure that the two organizations work in the closest possible harmony.

No.

Which two headings?

Mr. Chairman, the minister indicated in his reply a few moments ago that he recognized the real importance of the reserve units as they are spread out across the country. I am sure the minister is aware of the very excellent unit of the Royal Canadian Engineers established in the town of Kimberley. It is a mining community where a large percentage of the employees are engineers and others with mechanical training.
This unit is up to full strength but has completely inadequate facilities. They are renting an old hall which, while it has been of some use, has got well beyond its usefulness. For some time we have been pressing for an armoury. In addition, the unit has to pay high rent for storage of the equipment, trucks and the various armaments.
I was assured by the former minister that plans were well in hand for the establishment of an armoury in Kimberley for this very important unit. I have not seen any evidence of any progress. Can the minister tell me what the position is today?
The whole question of the construction of new armouries is under review at the present time, and the desirability of constructing an armoury at Kimberley is part of that review.
I am sure the minister will agree that it is important to maintain such a unit as this, which is highly trained in engineering, and that he should give primary consideration to an armoury there.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Shall the headings "Canadian army, regular and militia" carry?
It is one o'clock.

I have one or two questions to ask on the militia heading but I am sure it will take more than one minute to answer them. Will you call it one o'clock, Mr. Chairman?
At one o'clock the committee took recess.

AFTER RECESS

The committee resumed at 2.30 p.m.

Mr. Chairman, I have several questions to ask the Minister of National Defence, particularly with regard to the militia. Some of them were already answered this morning in reply to questions asked by various members on this side of the house. I was very much interested in hearing the comments of the minister this morning on the role of the militia. Before I proceed to ask questions I should like to give my understanding of what the minister said this morning in order that we will be able to proceed on a firm basis. I believe the minister stated that the militia is to continue in its role of an aid to the civil power. He stated further that the militia is not taking over civil defence but that because of its role as an aid to the civil power it is necessary for the militia to step up its training in civil defence and that this is actually being done. If I am wrong up to this point I should like the minister to correct me.
That is correct.
On the other hand, the militia is not to continue its old role of providing reserves in time of war but is being reorganized into mobile columns.
No, that is not correct. I have said that the secondary or alternative role of the militia will be to be prepared to supply reinforcements if ever required in time of war.

I thank the minister for the correction. I wanted to have the record straight. Is it correct that the purpose of the additional role of the militia involving reorganization into mobile columns is so that these columns can be shifted to adjacent theatres of action inside of Canada as those theatres may develop if war comes to Canada?

The militia is not being reorganized into support columns. The militia units are being called upon to earmark certain personnel in order to supply some units to the support columns. Let us take the Winnipeg unit. The Winnipeg Rifles might be asked to supply two rescue companies. The Fort Garry Horse might be asked to supply
Supply-National Defence a reconnaissance company for the support column in Winnipeg. The support column in Winnipeg might be required to render aid, shall we say, to the northern part of Winnipeg which perhaps had suffered a disaster or might be moved to Port Arthur or anywhere else where their assistance might be required.

I thank the minister very much for his explanation. I think the matter has been clarified. Would the minister also consider that these militia units, in addition to being mobile columns, might also become islands of resistance in case of Canada being overrun by an enemy? The immensity of this country makes it impossible for any enemy to overrun it everywhere at the same time. Having regard to the fact that the enemy might be subjected to attacks from our own bases or bases of our allies and might be subjected to being partially overrun, it would seem to me that by forming islands of resistance throughout the North American continent we could establish the core or the backbone, if you wish, of phase No. 2 in any world war. I am not one who believes in a war that will last only a few hours. The minister knows very well that unless you are dead they have to come and get you if you still want to fight. I should like to hear the opinion of the minister with regard to using the militia units as islands of resistance.

I am glad to say that the prospect of Canada or any part of Canada being overrun by invading forces is extremely remote. It would only occur after we had lost the battle of survival. Under those circumstances militia units and any other organized bodies would have to continue the struggle for survival and if any militia personnel were left they would be in a position to offer such centres of resistance as the hon. member has described. Therefore they are continuing their strictly military training as well as concentrating on training to render aid to the civil power during the first and what we believe is the crucial stage of the battle for survival.

I thank the minister again for his clarification. Would the minister tell us whether the savings which were announced and which I understand are created by a reduction of militia activity appear anywhere in the estimates now under review?

They will be reflected in the estimates for next year. There is one point I should like to emphasize. Canada now has a regular force of 49,000 soldiers. These men are serving for periods of three years and are then returning to civilian life as trained men. One can imagine that in the event of an
2356	HOUSE OF
Supply-National Defence emergency large numbers of these men, particularly those who had left the service more recently, would return to their units. Therefore there is now a much greater reserve of trained men in Canada, exclusive of the militia, than there has ever been before.

I would agree with the minister on that count as long as the militia units remain as active as possible wherever they are situated. If these men coming out from the regular forces have nowhere to go they will return to their civilian occupations and what they have learned in the armed forces will be lost. I should like to comment on that particular subject. Great concern has been expressed throughout the country about the unknown or somewhat unstable policy of the government regarding the militia. We have had to ask many questions on the subject during the question period and we are still asking questions. To use the minister's words, the minister said that the role of the militia used to be glamorous, phony or impractical, and I feel that the house and the Canadian people are justified in requesting an explanation from the minister of these words which he himself used in the house.

The minister never said that the role of the militia had ever been glamorous or phony. There is no glamour about modern war, none whatever. It would be purely phony to hold out to the militia the prospect of going over in the early days of a conflict to supply reinforcements to a European theatre of war.

I could not agree more with the last part of the minister's remarks. There could be nothing more phony than sending the militia abroad in time of war, unless it were a protracted war which we could not contemplate. I could not agree more with his earlier statements. However, I should like to quote from Hansard of October 16, 1957, page 38, when the minister was being asked a question about the militia. He said:
That may not be as glamorous a role as some of the other ones which have in the past been carried out by the militia, but X am confident that the militia will render the same patriotic service in this role as it has always done, rather than seeking some phony, glamorous role which hardly exists.
Those are the words the minister pronounced in the house.

There is no suggestion in those words that the militia has ever been asked to carry out any phony role. There was a glamorous role. Certainly, there was a certain amount of glamour to war in bygone days. There is no glamour in war today.

There again, I could not agree more with the minister. There is no glamour


about war. Certainly nobody wants to go to war. If we are discussing this matter at the present time, it is because we do not want any war. After all, the whole Department of National Defence is insurance for peace. But the minister is back-tracking on this statement which I quoted from Hansard. I will give him credit for that.
He did not back-track at all.
If it was back-tracking.

The minister said, again at page 38 of Hansard:
There is no suggestion of the militia having carried out in the past any role that could be considered as phony or glamorous, but there might be roles carried out in the future which would not be practical.
Later on, the minister said-

You get up
and make a speech on this if you want to.

Oh, shut up.

speechtext: Order.
Mr. Chairman, on October 22 I quoted these remarks in the house, and then I said this-
Oh, oh.

It would seem that I am hitting below the belt because I can hear noise from the other side. I said this as recorded at page 250 of Hansard for October 22, 1957:
I feel that the thousands of Canadian people who have sacrificed so many evenings, so many weekends and so many vacations during the summer time, purely as a result of devotion to duty to carry out training with the militia, deserve an explanation, and I trust this explanation will be forthcoming sooner than in mere due course.
Now, today we are gradually getting some explanation.

I wonder if the minister had an opportunity during the luncheon recess to look at today's copy of the Ottawa Citizen? If so, did he see in it a letter by Major General W. H. S. Macklin, retired, who is discussing a panel discussion which had taken place on T.V., and said:
My own wish, which wasn't debated either, was for a new and realistic defence policy for 1958.
In pursuit of our present sterile policy we have blown in billions on defence year after year. And yet as of new year's 1958, we are defenceless. We

have no defence whatever against the only direct attack that can be delivered on us-a nuclear attack.
We have only a deterrent, to maintain which we have already sacrificed every vestige of sovereign power to stay neutral as Dr. Whitton suggested we should do. Even the deterrent is now disastrously weakened by the Russian rocket.
For my part, in the absence of a new, and more objective defence policy, I should be delighted to take on the job of keeping Canada in her present helpless state for only nine hundred million per year, instead of the eighteen hundred millions or more that we have been dumping into the quicksands of the defence department year by year in the past.
I imagine, Mr. Chairman, that the minister will have a better estimate than I have of the authority with which General Macklin speaks. Both of them being major generals they should have a fair estimate of each other's ability. I should like to ask the minister if he agrees, in the first place, with General Macklin's statement that:
We have no defence whatever against the only direct attack that can be delivered on us-a nuclear attack.
I should like to ask him if he agrees that is the only sort of attack to which we could be subjected. If so, does he seriously contend that there is any method by which, at the present time, Canada or her allies could have a deterrent which might prevent such an attack. I know this morning he told me that they did have a means of protecting the bases from which deterrent attacks could be launched. I would think that is rather questionable in the light of his further statement that there is no defence against the intercontinental guided missile, no method by which the launching sites for deterrents against them could be protected. I wonder, Mr. Chairman, if the minister would care to comment on General Macklin's rather forthright statement that we have literally no defence, and at the moment we are dumping billions down the drain in pursuit of the same sterile policies?

Mr. Chairman, I thought we were dealing with the details of the army estimates. This question gets back again into the realm of general policy. In so far as the statement of General Macklin is concerned, I did not have an opportunity of reading it during the luncheon hour. I have known General Macklin for a period of 30 years or more, and I think I am in a position to assess the reliability of the information that he sometimes gives to the general public through newspaper reports. I disagree entirely with him that we are in a helpless state. The whole tenor of the NATO conference was that we are speaking from a position of strength. NATO, of which Canada is a partner and an important partner,
Supply-National Defence speaks not from weakness, not from craven fear, not with any idea of appeasement, but from strength and in the knowledge that Russia is fully aware of the strength that there is in the powers of retaliation. That is our hope for peace. So long as we keep up that strength I give the Russians sufficient credit for common sense that they are not going to attempt to attack this country. We count, for the preservation of peace, on the knowledge that we are prepared, if necessary and if Russia violates the present peace conditions-the west has no thought of offensive operations-we are yet in a position to strike back in a way that certainly would not make it worth Russia's while to do that.
I admit that we have no direct defence at the present time against the intercontinental missile, nor has Russia got any strength in intercontinental missiles at the present time. Perhaps by the time Russia has developed strength which might make her foolhardy enough to attack this country we shall have the answer to the intercontinental missile. But our hope for peace today rests on the power of our alliance, on the deterrent that that alliance is able to provide, and on the means of retaliation if Russia is so indiscreet as to start a war.

Earlier this morning the minister was kind enough to indicate that our expenditure to maintain the army in Europe was about $30 million and for the air force, $90 million. Again, if I may, I should like to refer him to the speech he delivered in July, 1956 in which he suggested, as recorded at the bottom of page 6207 of Hansard of that year:
I am not suggesting that there should be any cuts or reductions made in this year's estimates, but I think between now and the time the minister presents his estimates a year hence he must review the whole situation in a most thorough and comprehensive manner.
I would remind him that his colleagues the Minister of Veterans Affairs and the Secretary of State supported him two years ago in expressing the hope at least that some relief could be seen in the future toward reducing these very heavy expenditures. Now that the minister has been in charge of the department for six months I wonder if he could indicate whether any effective savings have been made in connection with the retaining of the armed services in Europe. While we are not discussing the air force at the moment, these two items total $120 million. While the minister was very careful two years ago to indicate that no intelligent person would suggest that those who are serving Canada in Europe should have their pay and allowances or other services cut, the whole tenor of the minister's remarks two years ago indicated

Supply

National Defence that $120 million a year was a very heavy drain on the Canadian economy and that something should be done to reduce this amount. Could the minister indicate what has happened in the last 12 months or in the year 1957? Has there been any effective reduction in our expenditure with respect to maintaining the army and the air force in Europe?

This applies to the air force. Quite recently arrangements have been made to extend the period of service of the personnel in Europe, thereby eliminating the amount of transportation and the cost of continually changing the personnel. They were on a basis of a two-year term of service. But now, where there is any desire on the part of an individual or if the individual has no objection, his period of service is to be extended to three or four years. We are considering the possibility of introducing a similar sort of rotation with respect to the army. Wherever possible we have been reducing administrative costs, which reductions have enabled us to cover the increases which it was desirable to pay to the troops in the way of pay and allowances. But I admit frankly that it is a heavy drain on the Canadian economy to keep these forces in Europe. However it is an obligation that we have assumed. We believe it is money well spent in order to preserve the peace of the world.
Two years ago the minister, as a private member and as an ex-soldier, expressed the considered opinion that these items should be carefully reviewed.

They have been carefully
reviewed.

Can the minister indicate the percentage of the reduction in expenses? He has had six months as minister. He gave us roughly the figure of $120 million a year as what it has been costing. Could he indicate in percentages roughly the savings that are going to be effected as a result of the careful survey to which he has referred? Can he give us the total amount or the percentage of reduction that he anticipates?

We have not it in detail yet. The end of the year will reflect what savings we have been able to make. If it is possible to make any savings in that respect, they will be reflected in next year's estimates.
This morning when we were discussing the matter of improving the site at Camp Chippewa the minister indicated he might give me an answer after lunch.

Yes. During the luncheon hour I was able to make some inquiries with regard to Chippewa. I understand that

the buildings at that camp, which was established during the Korean crisis, are owned by the Department of National Defence but that the land is owned by the city of North Bay. It has been agreed that the Department of National Defence will return part of the land to the city and will purchase the remainder. It has also been agreed that there will be carried out certain improvements, which I have described this morning more or less as general maintenance, to the buildings and their surroundings. I am informed that the plans have not yet been finalized for these improvements but that as soon as they are finalized the necessary improvements and developments of the surroundings will be undertaken.

I should like to thank the minister for this information. With that thanks I should like also to couple the suggestion that perhaps he and his officials could expedite the matter. At the present time there are over 2,300 unemployed in our city. This figure is comparable to 900 unemployed exactly a year ago. My point in saying that is this. The majority of the people who are unemployed in our area at the present time are from the construction trades. If some of this work could be carried out at an early date I think it might be helpful.
I will certainly look into that matter and see whether we can start the work at an early date. We should like to take advantage of any possible opportunity to relieve unemployment.

At
the bottom of page 330 and at the top of page 331 there are listed a number of positions simply under the title "assistants". The salaries or wages paid to these assistants vary from about $1,100 at Belgrade to over $4,000 at Washington. Can the minister say what kind of assistants these persons are or what sort of work it is which they do for these varying rates of pay?
In the main they are civilian clerks and stenographers who are attached to the military attaches at these various stations. I believe that is correct.
What kind of a person would be working for $1,100 a year?
It would depend entirely on the country. In the main-I do not say exclusively-they are nationals of the countries in which they are employed.

I note that in the estimates for the navy there is listed an item "All other expenditures, $1,125,000" and for the army, $4,256,000.
The Depuiy Chairman: Order. May I call the hon. member's attention to the fact that he is now talking about a navy item which was passed yesterday.
Then I will restrict myself to the item for the army, "All other expenditures, $4,256,000". If possible, could the minister itemize this statement?

The main items under that heading are laundry and dry cleaning. There is an item for $1,069,000 under that. There is also photography and aerial mapping-a large program of mapping is carried out- and that is an item amounting to $1,070,000. There are special grants for uniforms, equipment for bands, compensation for loss of property and various miscellaneous items amounting to $584,730, making a total of $4,250,000. These are a large number of miscellaneous items not otherwise classified.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: That brings us to the Northwest highway system on page 335, the last item under "Army". Is it agreed that we proceed on that basis?
Agreed.
I wonder whether the minister could bring us up to date with regard to any recent developments in the Northwest highway system, particularly with regard to the matter of the bridge replacement.

Unfortunately the bridge over the Peace river between Dawson Creek and Fort St. John was washed out as a result of very heavy rains in the early fall and the general erosion of the north bank. This bridge, it will be recalled, was built by United States engineers during the war. It has been necessary to make temporary arrangements in order that the traffic in the area round Fort St. John and Dawson Creek might be continued. It is mainly civilian traffic; there is very little army traffic going over that portion of the highway at the present time. By various means and by making temporary arrangements for the P.G.E. bridge, thanks to the co-operation of the British Columbia government traffic has been resumed. A small additional bridge had to be built over the Pine river so that traffic could get to the south end of the P.G.E. bridge. A board of consultants has now been established under the chairmanship of Dr. P. L. Pratley, a well-known Montreal engineering consultant, Mr. H. H. Minshall, a Vancouver consultant, Mr. A. B. Sanderson of Victoria, 96698-181
Supply-National Defence and Mr. L. G. Grimble of Edmonton, all of whom are well known engineering consultants.
They have held one meeting already in Ottawa and the second meeting is to take place on January 8 in Vancouver. It is hoped they will produce a design for a more suitable type of bridge than the one which has been in existence, and as soon as a design has been produced it is the intention of the department to call for tenders and to restore the bridge at the earliest possible opportunity.
Mr. Chairman, I have from time to time seen press reports about certain plans for hard surfacing of certain portions of the Alaska highway-
Tenders have been let for that portion of the highway between Dawson Creek and Fort St. John, and the work is now in progress.
Has that portion of the highway been turned over to the province of British Columbia, or will it remain under the jurisdiction of the Northwest highway authorities?

It will remain under the jurisdiction of the federal government until it has been hard surfaced and then it is hoped that discussions will take place with the province of British Columbia to see whether the province would be willing to take over that portion of the highway, which is of very little defence value at the present time, it being used mainly for commercial operations.
Is the Department of National Defence bearing the entire cost of the hard surfacing program?

The Department of National Defence is bearing the entire cost of the surfacing of the highway because it was in the original agreement that we had to maintain this highway and it has been found that owing to the very heavy wear and tear on the gravel highway the cost of keeping it gravelled, and repairing it, was more than the over-all cost of hard surfacing.
Is there any study under way on the question of proceeding with a surfacing program farther north on the highway?
No, there is not the same heavy traffic north of Fort St. John as there is between Fort St. John and Dawson Creek.
