speechtext:
We are now proceeding to the item concerning defence services, air, at the top of page 339, an item which continues until about half way down the page on page 346.

Supply-National Defence

Mr. Chairman, perhaps this is the occasion on which to ask some questions in the hope of receiving some clarification in regard to North American air defence headquarters, on NORAD as it is more popularly known. Earlier questions on this matter, both in the house and in the committee on external affairs, have made it clear that there is no political agreement between the two governments laying down the principles upon which this headquarters should operate, and the relationship of the headquarters to the two governments, and that omission seems to us to be a very notable one because of the importance of this development, an importance which is perhaps as much political as it is military.
We did learn at one stage that the headquarters was operating under an interim arrangement. Then later on December 5 the minister pointed out, as recorded in Hansard at page 1941, that this was not even an interim arrangement in the sense that anything had been put down on paper to govern this matter. He said he would prefer to call the arrangement "interim discussions rather than notes" and he went on to say there had been no passing of any formal notes at all, but there had been visits to the government of the United States.
I take it, Mr. Chairman, that steps are, however, being taken to work out a political arrangement which would govern this very important development, and I should like as my first question to ask the minister what progress has been made in regard to such a political arrangement and whether it has yet been concluded. The minister indicated at one stage, I believe, a hope that it would be concluded by the beginning of the year. Can he tell the committee what progress has been made in this matter?

Yes. I saw Air Marshall Slemon who visited me in Ottawa a few days ago and he said that progress is being made in the working out of these notes. There has already been a draft note submitted which we have sent back to Washington with certain comments. The last information I received was that this matter would be discussed by the United States joint staffs not before January 10.
Mr. Chairman, is this intergovernmental agreement which by its very nature would have to be a political agreement being worked out merely by the two defence departments of the governments concerned?

No, no. They are drawing up first drafts which of course will be submitted to the governments. As the hon.
[The Deputy Chairman.]
gentleman knows these international agreements take a surprisingly long time.

That is true, Mr. Chairman, but there has been a period of six months in which to conclude this agreement because the headquarters has been in operation for six months without any agreement interim or otherwise.
May I ask another question. It was stated in this house by the Prime Minister before the recess that as a result of the NATO council meeting in Paris "NORAD had become an integral part of the NATO military structure". Those were the words used. I would be grateful if the minister would explain how that has been done and what is the actual relationship then between NORAD and NATO which makes it an integral part of the NATO military structure which I must say was surprising news to me?

As the hon. gentleman will recall when the NATO organization was first set up there were I think five regional areas established one of which was the Canada-United States regional planning group. NORAD is definitely under that Canada-United States regional planning group. They report to that Canada-United States regional planning group. That regional planning group differs from the organization in Europe in that it does not have a supreme commander. It consists of the chiefs of staffs of the two countries, Canada and the United States. It has never been considered desirable either by this government or by the previous government to appoint a supreme commander of that particular area. Therefore you have this regional planning group consisting of the chiefs of staff of Canada and the chiefs of staff of the United States. They report to the military committee of NATO and they in turn report to their respective governments and in that way NORAD is definitely a part of the NATO structure.

Mr. Chairman, what the minister has stated and stated very clearly is of course not new. That has been the situation now for some years. But there is a very great difference as the minister will undoubtedly appreciate-and indeed he has already indicated that there is a difference- between a NATO command and the Canada-United States planning group. There is no similarity between the two except in the sense that the planning group, as the minister pointed out, does report annually its activities to the military committee of NATO, but to give the impression that the Canada-United States planning group and

NORAD under that group is in the same relationship to NATO as a NATO command is of course misleading.
Only yesterday I received through the courtesy of the secretary general of NATO an end of the year publication called "Facts about NATO" in which the following paragraph occurs:
A Canada-United States regional planning group has existed ever since the signing of the Ogdens-burg Agreement in 1940 by Canada and the United States. It was a consultative body which, after having functioned successfully during world war II, was asked in 1949 to put forward, within the framework of over-all NATO strategy, defence plans for the Canada-United States area. It is mainly concerned with questions of defence against air attack in the Arctic regions and with the establishment of a vast radar network stretching from Alaska to Newfoundland. The Arctic defence operation is a joint Canadian-United States effort, and the stations may be manned by Canadian or United States staff, or by combined Canadian-United States personnel.
The NATO report then goes on to say:
The Canada-United States regional planning group has no assigned forces and is not a command in the real sense of the word. Its primary task is to work out a common strategy for the North American area.
The NATO commands are definitely under the control of the NATO organization and not only report to but receive political and military guidance from the NATO organization, but NORAD of course has no relationship of that kind to NATO as I am sure my hon. friend will admit because he himself stated that in the house on December 5, 1957, as recorded at page 1899 of Hansard when he said:
The officer appointed to fill the position of commander in chief. North American air defence, was made responsible to the governments of both countries for the air defence of North America, and to report directly to the United States joint chiefs of staff and the Canadian chiefs of staff committee. All plans for the deployment and employment of air defence forces must be approved by the chiefs of staff and, when necessary, by the governments of both countries.
There is no reference, of course, to NATO in that paragraph and therefore the impression that may have been created by the words of the Prime Minister that NORAD is now an integral part of NATO seems to me to be an inaccurate one. The fact is, of course, that NORAD, as I understand it, does not derive its authority in any way, shape or form from NATO. To follow that up and arising out of the paragraph which I have just read from the statement the minister gave the house on December 5 I would like to ask him the following questions.
Does the commander or the deputy commander of NORAD receive his appointment from any NATO agency? The answer to this is obvious from what the minister has already said. Secondly, does the commander or the 96698-181J
Supply-National Defence deputy commander of NORAD derive his authority from the NATO council or any other NATO agency? If the answers to those two questions are in the negative, as I am sure they are judging from the minister's previous statement, what then is the source of the authority and command of the NORAD commander and deputy commander? Perhaps the minister might reply to those questions.

The commander of NORAD, General Partridge, of course was appointed by the United States in exactly the same way as the deputy commander, Air Marshal Slemon, was appointed by this government. Both of them are working together at Colorado Springs. The concept of this North American defence command is very definitely part of the whole NATO attempt to prevent war developing.
I think it is utterly impossible to separate the defence of the North American continent from the rest of the NATO defence plan. This command has been set up under the general Canada-United States planning group. As the hon. gentleman said, that planning group has been set up ever since NATO was started and I understand that one of the objects of all of these planning groups and of all of these regional planning groups was the protection of the particular area with which they were concerned. It is only a later development that commanders-in-chief were appointed for some of the other commands. That did not exist, I believe, when the regional pacts were first started and they have gradually developed.
As I pointed out, there is no commander-in-chief of the Canada-United States pact, but the joint chiefs of staff of Canada and of the United States act in that capacity and refer not only to their own governments but to the military committees of NATO. I think the chain of command is identical with the chain of command of some subordinate commander in the European force who, instead of reporting to a committee, owing to the particular situation existing in the group, reports to the commander-in-chief, General Norstad, who in turn reports to the military committee. The chain of command is identical; the purposes are identical; but it has not yet been considered desirable to establish a supreme commander of the Canadian-United States regional pact.

Mr. Chairman, I quite agree that these various aspects of defence are interdependent and indeed they are indivisible. One of my preoccupations with this matter is that action has not been taken to bring this particular command into closer relationship with the NATO command.
28S2

Supply-National Defence
The minister had indicated that there is really no difference in essence between the NATO command as such and this North American air defence organization but he knows that in relation to the NATO command we in this parliament know exactly where we stand. There was a political agreement between governments establishing NATO and its commands. That agreement was discussed and approved in this house and as a result of that approval Canadian forces were allocated to a NATO commander appointed by NATO though on the recommendation, in so far as SACEUR is concerned, of the United States government. It was all done in a perfectly regular parliamentary way with a political foundation for the action which we took.
As I understand it, nothing like that has happened in so far as NORAD is concerned. It was taken by governmental action without any political agreement, though one is being worked out now. It was taken without bringing this particular command into any other relationship with NATO than that, and it is a very tenuous relationship, with all respect to the minister, which comes through its association with the United States-Canada planning group. I think it is quite misleading to give the impression that the same kind of action was taken in setting up NORAD as was taken in setting up SACEUR. We, of course, participate in both. We know where we stand in one; we do not know where we stand-at least, I do not know where we stand -in the other.
For instance, the minister has already said in this house that General Partridge, the commander of NORAD, a commander-I may be wrong in this-who I believe has no obligation whatever to report to any NATO agency as has general Norstad; and, whose deputy is a Canadian, has operational control over the air forces allocated for the defence of North America, whether they are United States or Canadian air forces. That being the case, surely it is important for us to know from what source this commander derives the authority which gives him operational command over Canadian forces. We know the source of that authority in the case of General Norstad and the NATO command; we do not know it in the case of NORAD.
General Partridge, however, seems himself to know the source of his own authority because he has stated that the President of the United States has given his approval to use, without reference to anybody, any weapons at his disposal if there is a hostile aircraft in the sky. That is what General Partridge said as I read it from an interview he gave a few weeks ago. One of the weapons that General Partridge has at his

disposal is the Royal Canadian Air Force. Therefore I would like to know whether General Partridge has the same authority from the Canadian government and how he got it. Furthermore, I would like to know whether the deputy commander, Air Marshal Slemon, if he were in charge, and he would be in charge if General Partridge were away, has exactly the same authority and command over United States operational forces as has General Partridge.

I can assure the hon. member at once that Air Marshal Slemon is in every respect the deputy commander. If General Partridge is away Air Marshal Slemon has full control of the United States air force designed for the defence of the North American continent.
Will the minister answer my other question? What is the source of General Partridge's authority and his operational control over Canadian forces?

That will be laid out in detail in the formal note. At the present time we are operating, as the hon. member said, on an oral and verbal agreement. The two commanders are there. They are getting acquainted with each other and it is very important that these two staffs should work in together. There is, I am assured from what Air Marshal Slemon told me, the greatest possible harmony and co-operation between the two groups at Colorado Springs. If anything happened within the next day or two that headquarters would be in a position to render a defence of this country which could never have been achieved, the magnitude of it could never have been achieved, if there had not been an integrated command.

I agree with the minister that it is of the very greatest importance that these two forces should work together in harmony and that they should be able to work swiftly in an emergency. I am sure there is no difference between us on that score. I do not necessarily agree with him, however, in his last observation that they are now in a position to act so much more swiftly and effectively than they were before NORAD was set up.
They are.

As the minister knows, before NORAD was established there were very effective arrangements in connection with cooperation between the air defence forces of the two countries and I cannot follow the minister when he seems to indicate that all of this can be done-though it is very important that it should be done-merely by an oral or verbal arrangement between members

of the two governments. That seems to me to be a very shaky basis for the kind of cooperation which is so important both militarily and politically.
As I have explained, those oral conversations and agreements will be confirmed by a formal note which will be placed before parliament in due course.

Mr. Chairman, I should like to indicate once again our support of the concern which has been expressed by the hon. member for Algoma East. We agree that it is desirable to have joint defence of these two countries and that the necessary arrangements should be worked out. But we also feel it is extremely important that the proper political basis be established for any action that might be taken by such a joint defence force. I too was interested in the words that the Prime Minister used in this connection on December 21 after his return from Paris, and I think it is worthwhile to place on the record what he said on that occasion. To do so is to point up the fact to which the hon. member for Algoma East has already referred, namely that in our view there is something a bit misleading in these remarks. This is what the Prime Minister said as found on page 2721 of Hansard:
I refer to the arrangements we made with the United States government for the integrated air defence of North America under what is called NORAD. I want to re-emphasize that I pointed out there, and it was accepted as a fact, that these integrated forces are an integral part of the NATO military structure in the Canada-United States region; that there is a committee of NATO dealing with Canada-United States relations in this regard, and that anything we have done has been reported to the standing group and that course will be followed in the future. The NATO council will have full reports on everything we do, similar to the practice followed in all other NATO military commands.
These words, Mr. Chairman, suggest that there is a similarity between the control over NORAD and the control over other NATO commands such as SACEUR. Yet when one reads these words closely it is quite clear that there is a difference. The Prime Minister did not allege in his remarks that NORAD derives its authority from NATO as is the case with General Norstad who is in charge in Europe but merely that Canada and the United States had vis-a-vis NORAD reported to the Canada-United States political group and in turn reported to NATO. It is one thing to derive authority from a civilian body such as the NATO council and it is another thing simply to report the activities of a military group to such a body.
Supply-National Defence
It seems to me that in this matter we are dealing with something that is extremely important and very basic to our whole democratic approach. Some of us have been in the house long enough to remember the days of the slogan that the parliament of Canada will decide what Canada will do so far as any outbreak of war is concerned. We remember how Mr. King used to give us that assurance very categorically. That, of course, was in the days when wars were launched or declared by nations as individuals. Nevertheless, so long as that was the situation we preserved parliamentary control over this country going to war by means of a section in the National Defence Act which requires that if the government of the day puts troops on active service outside of Canada parliament, if it is not then in session, must be called within a certain number of days. In other words, parliament must be given the opportunity to approve or otherwise of the action of the government which is superior to the armed forces.
We, of course, had that in the case of the outbreak of war in 1939. As a matter of fact, parliament was called within a day or so of the troops being put on active service. We also had it at the time troops were sent to Korea. An order in council was passed and parliament was summoned within the required length of time. Orders in council were passed when troups were sent to Europe under NATO, and so on. In other words, in these developing arrangements we have held to the principle that the civilian authority is superior to the military authority.
In the case of NATO we got away a bit from the necessity of parliament being called in the event that something should happen in Europe. Our troops are already there but they are over there under a political command to which parliament has agreed because we have had the NATO treaty before the House of Commons.
When we come to the situation we are now discussing, the possibility of joint operational activities on the part of the United States and Canadian air forces, these could happen by the decision of a United States general or a Canadian air marshal. They could happen because of discussions that have taken place not even at the departmental level but between military people in these two countries without parliament having agreed in advance to the necessary arrangements.
It seems to me that even the exchange of notes that the minister says will take place in due course is not sufficient. It seems to me that we must either have the situation

Supply-National Defence that we had in years gone by whereby parliament is summoned if our forces have been put on active service or we must have an agreement in advance such as the approval by parliament of the North Atlantic treaty. In the light of the seriousness of this whole matter I feel that the assurances the minister has given still are not satisfactory. Like the hon. member for Algoma East, we agree that these arrangements have to be made. We agree as to the desirability of joint defence. But we also emphasize very strongly the need of maintaining civilian political authority over the military operations.
When General Norstad visited this country a few months ago and spoke both publicly and privately at various places in Ottawa he made it very clear that he has military authority only because he derives that authority from NATO. The minister has not yet demonstrated to us that General Partridge and Air Marshal Slemon draw their military authority from any civilian or political group. It is not satisfactory to say that they get their authority from the joint chiefs of staff of the two countries. The minister says that in the event of action there might be a telephone call to Washington or Ottawa but the basic requirement of establishing political authority over the military establishment has not yet been made clear.
As I say, it seems to us that even the exchange of notes between the two governments which is envisaged is not sufficient and that soon or later there should be either an agreement that somehow is within the framework of NATO in the same way as the other commands, so that authority is derived from the civilian side of NATO, or there should be something in the nature of a treaty between the United States and Canada which parliament will have the opportunity to consider in the same way that we have considered the North Atlantic treaty and other arrangements of this kind.
Let no one suggest that either the hon. member for Algoma East or we in this group are holding back so far as joint defence arrangements are concerned. But we do suggest most strongly that the proper political authority for such defence arrangements should be established and that parliament should have the chance to approve those arrangements.
I agree entirely with the hon. member that political authority must be established and it is established.
Where?

The chiefs of staff of Canada report to me as Minister of National Defence. I report to the cabinet defence committee or

to the cabinet as a whole. That is where political authority is maintained in exactly the same way as the joint chiefs of staff of the United States report to their political authorities. In addition, the combined chiefs of staff report to the military committee of NATO which reports to the military council of NATO. Now, that is where the civilian control is maintained, and the plans which are made have to be examined and approved in principle by the civilian control side in the United States or in Canada.
I am afraid that the hon. member is picturing a possibility of these forces being sent away from this continent. These are the forces, the Canadian air force and the United States air force, specially earmarked for the defence of this North American continent. They are not going to move away from this North American continent, but they will go into action if at any time enemy bombers commit an overt act of war by flying through Canadian air space and giving indication they are about to commit a hostile act. They go into operation automatically. There would be no opportunity to call parliament together when enemy bombers were over our territory. You have to make these arrangements beforehand, and these arrangements are made beforehand. These forces are ready to go into action if any enemy bombers violate our air space and show a hostile intention against the North American continent.

No
one ever suggested that the phrase "Parliament will decide" meant that parliament had actually to be summoned between the time the enemy attacked and retaliation was commenced for the defence of Canada. The way in which the role of parliament to decide has been preserved is that within a certain period of time after the forces have been put on active service or given a job to do parliament must meet. But we have gone beyond that. We have now got to the point where we have made certain commitments, such as the North Atlantic Treaty, which would make it possible for forces responsible to NATO to go into action and parliament not be called because we have already agreed to the terms of the treaty.
But in this instance there is not anything to which the parliament of Canada has had any opportunity of agreeing so far as this joint defence of North America is concerned. The minister says I seem to be picturing these forces being used elsewhere than in North America. Well, at any rate a number of our personnel are outside of Canada right now. They are down at Colorado Springs. The minister might say it is only a handful, 35 or 40 service personnel, but whatever the number might be I would point out that they

are outside of Canada. In any previous instance where troops have been put on active service outside of Canada there has been an order in council and that order in council has been tabled in parliament within the required number of days of the order in council being issued. So far we have been able to learn of only one order in council that has anything to do with the setup at Colorado Springs, and that is the order in council stipulating what Air Marshal Slemon's salary and allowances are to be.
In the very nature of the case defence could involve Canadian air force personnel in operations outside of the territorial limits of Canada. I am not objecting to that being done. I recognize a situation could arise in which that would be necessary, and in which it would be necessary for that action to be taken instantly without the opportunity for the parliamentary process. But it is because of the necessity for that that it seems to me a special decision should be made in advance and parliament should have an opportunity of making that decision.
There is one other question I should like to put to the minister. In view of the fact that General Partridge is in command of these tremendous forces which are based at Colorado Springs, and in view of the obvious interest of General Partridge and his associates in the defence of the position of the United States, what would happen if United States interests or forces in the Far East were attacked? What would happen, for example, if any trouble broke out between the mainland of China and Formosa and United States forces in Formosa were under attack and General Partridge felt it necessary to dispatch bombers from Colorado Springs?
General Partridge has no authority whatever outside of the defence of the North American continent. If there is action in Formosa it would not come under General Partridge.

May I put the question this way? What would happen if there was action in Formosa or off Formosa between the United States and the communist regime in China, and as a result of that action in the Far East there were steps taken by the communist regime in China which indicated an air threat to this continent and General Partridge interpreted it as such? Would he then have authority to put the continental air defences into operation, including the Canadian element of his command?

I am quite certain that would be a point which would have to be covered by political agreement beforehand. The idea of General Partridge's command is for the
Supply-National Defence defence of the North American continent. I suggest that if the North American continent is being attacked by anybody Canada is within that target area. We would have to have defensive measures taken in Canada as well as in the United States.

I quite agree that we have to have these defensive measures, and of course we should take them on a continental basis. All we on this side are seeking to establish is the authority for action of this kind, the political authority. I agree with what the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre has said. You have to have these political arrangements made in advance. In an emergency there will be no time for calling parliament, perhaps there will be no time for even making a telephone call, as was once suggested. But there are various ways of making these advance political arrangements. We did it one way in the case of NATO, not only by government decision but by parliamentary decision.
The political authority for the integration of the North American air command, it has been clearly established now, was a decision of the government which decision has not been approved or even discussed by parliament. We have nothing to discuss because the political arrangements covering that decision made by the government six months ago are still under negotiation. Until we have an opportunity to consider the results of the negotiation the action that has been taken has no parliamentary backing of any kind; that is obvious.
May I ask the minister, while I am on my feet, two questions. One is, when was the establishment of NORAD reported to NATO and, secondly, is it the intention of the government, when agreement has been reached with the United States on the political arrangements covering this defence organization, to submit that political agreement to the NATO council for discussion with the NATO partners in the hope perhaps that an agreement of this kind could be made an integral part of the NATO organization? Perhaps NORAD could be brought into closer relationship with NATO than seems at present to be the case.
NATO was informed prior to the publication or prior to the joint announcement made by myself and the defence secretary of the United States. I have not the exact date.
Was it prior to the decision taken by the Canadian government?

No, it would not be prior to the decision made by the Canadian government but it would be prior to the statement

Supply-National Defence which was given. As to the second part of the question, that matter of course would have to be discussed with the United States. I could not make any firm commitment. I could only express a personal opinion which it would not be wise for me to express here. It would have to be discussed, as the hon. gentleman knows, with the United States.

There are one or
two questions that I should like to ask. It seems to me that some of the important questions put by the hon. member for Algoma East have not yet been answered. It is true that the hon. member for Algoma East said that the putting of the interrogations themselves likely reveals the answers. He asked two questions in this context. One was this. Do the commanders in question, namely General Partridge and Air Marshal Slemon, derive their authority from a NATO agency? There has been no answer to that question. He also asked this question: does their authority derive only, in so far as Canada is concerned, from an oral expression given by the minister or by the government itself? I think the Minister of National Defence is confronted with the necessity of answering those questions, even though their replies may be self-evident.
There is another question that arises out of a statement made by the Minister of National Defence in answer to a question put by the hon. member for Algoma East. The hon. member for Algoma East asked this question:	in the absence of General
Partridge, what authority will Air Marshal Slemon be capable of exercising? The Minister of National Defence at once rose and said, "Of course, in the absence of General Partridge, Air Marshal Slemon will have precisely the same authority that General Partridge himself would have".
That is correct.

The minister now says, "That is correct". That creates a very serious situation, it seems to me, because of what we are advised by General Partridge himself in the interview which he gave on September 6, and which is contained in the U.S. News and World Report. In that article, as I reminded the minister on another occasion in this house, General Partridge said in effect that he had an understanding with the President of the United States to the effect that there likely being no time available in the event of an emergency he was not obligated before acting to receive the informal or formal approval of the President or of the government of the United States. When asked as to the authority of General Partridge vis-a-vis the Canadian

government my hon. and gallant friend said that that kind of freedom of action in so far as Canada was concerned did not exist in so far as the NORAD commander was concerned, and that there would have to be consultation with Ottawa. We were never told who in Ottawa must be consulted. We were never told whether that was the Prime Minister, the Minister of National Defence or any combination of ministers of the crown. But in any event the point is that General Partridge, in so far as Canada is concerned, just could not on his own initiative and discretion push the button. 1 think I correctly state the situation as related by the Minister of National Defence to us some weeks ago.
If that is the case, what is the situation that now flows from the replies of my hon. friend? Air Marshal Slemon, a Canadian officer, No. 2 in command, will have in the United States and over United States air forces authority which he does not possess in Canada over Canadian air force officers and over the particular operation in the event of an emergency. This surely reveals the difficult position in which the minister finds himself and with which I think we all have much sympathy but I think it is largely based upon the character and the nature of the replies which he gave. Surely the situation in Canada with respect to this matter cannot be any different from the situation that prevails in the United States. This must, I would think, be conceived of as the same operation. Any decision taken by General Partridge or, in his absence, by Air Marshal Slemon must in the very nature of things apply to both countries. But it cannot do so, in so far as Canada is concerned, if what the minister said is to be taken as the correct procedural situation. I think the minister owes it to the country, to himself and to parliament to indicate whether or not the functions of General Partridge or, in his absence, of Air Marshal Slemon, are any different as between one country and another.
It surely must mean that General Partridge has in Canada precisely the same authority that he has in the United States. I think the minister also owes it to us to say whether or not the situation is as General Partridge revealed in this interview, namely that there would in all probability be no time for consultation; and if there is not time for consultation, does the minister still take the position that General Partridge, or in his absence, Air Marshal Slemon, must first of all contact someone in Ottawa? Also, as I say, the minister must tell us what particular authority in Ottawa.
All of this adds up to what the hon. member for Algoma East said, namely that these are

matters that require precision of agreement. The minister said that Air Marshal Slemon had gone to the United States and was working out an interim arrangement. He has not yet indicated to us whether, as the result of that interim arrangement leading to some kind of formal agreement between the United States and Canada, that agreement will at some subsequent time be submitted to parliament for approval or ratification. I would think, however, in view of the discussion that has taken place here today and during the course of this present session of parliament this government would not make the mistake even at this date of failing to bring to parliament a treaty or a document which embodies the policy which the government is prepared to recommend to parliament.
The Minister of National Defence said that this was not a matter involving the dispatch of troops overseas. I suppose technically that is correct, although under certain conceivable circumstances it could be the case that men employed in the defence of the country in this particular arrangement might have to leave the shores of Canada. That may or may not be an academic question but that surely is not the issue. When in November of 1940 the then prime minister of Canada submitted the Ogdensburg agreement that set up a joint board for defence between the United States and Canada that was an instrument that had nothing at all to do with the dispatch of troops anywhere, either on this continent or in Europe. But the government of the day took the parliamentary step of submitting to parliament the policy of the government in asking for approval. That is what the hon. member for Algoma East, the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre and others during the course of this particular discussion have insisted was a necessary thing to do within our parliamentary tradition.
In fact, our parliamentary tradition in Canada goes beyond that. Since 1926 there has grown up the custom, respected by every government, that any matters involving relations of this country, except commercial treaties, whether they include the dispatch of troops overseas or whether they are in the nature of commitments entered into by this country with other nations, should be submitted to parliament. We had a discussion in 1935 as to whether or not, for instance, the imposition of sanctions under the covenant of the League of Nations, if supported by Canada, would require first of all the consent, or the approval rather, of the Canadian parliament. If it is our tradition that this should be done in the case of nonmilitary action such as the sanctions which were contemplated in the case of the Ethio-pian-Italian dispute, then surely a matter of 96698-182
Supply-National Defence the greatest importance such as this, which is perhaps an agreement more important than any other agreement outside the NATO agreement that we have ever had to deal with, should be submitted to the parliament of Canada.
I think one could successfully argue that once a decision has been taken even in interim form-a decision which the Prime Minister said was a decision of the government as a whole-it should have been submitted to parliament. But it was not submitted to parliament. Even to this very day there has been no formal submission of the step taken, and now that the defence forces of the two countries are negotiating an agreement which will later be embodied, presumably as the hon. member for Algoma East has said in a political agreement-and the minister ought, I think, to give us an assurance about that-this surely will be submitted to parliament. Not that parliament objects to the objectives which the government has in mind, because it is elementary to observe that in this thermonuclear age it is essential for our continental defence that there should be the fullest co-operation between Canada and the United States, as the hon. member for Algoma East said. But nevertheless because of all the implications- implications which all of us appreciate without spelling them out-I think it is a desirable safeguard that, first of all, the government should have taken parliament into its confidence. This not having been done, we should at least be given an assurance that once a political document, whether in the form of an exchange of notes or a treaty is prepared, it will be submitted to parliament. The government will have decided its policy and I have no doubt what the result will be, but we will then be in a position to make an examination of all the factors involved.
But I think the minister will want to take this opportunity of acknowledging that the answers which General Partridge made are inconsistent with the replies he himself made a few weeks ago. Either General Partridge is right or the minister is wrong. Both cannot be right. I am sure the minister-and I say this to him knowing his heavy responsibility -must agree that this is the case. I understand that that interview between General Partridge and the interviewer was submitted after the end of June to either the minister, or if not to him, then to the Department of National Defence-I do not know whether I should say for approval. But I think that under the article there is a footnote-an asterisk on the first page-which says that the article, in so far as the Canadian references are concerned, was submitted to the

Supply-National Defence Department of National Defence in Canada. If this is the case I think the minister owes it to the house and to himself to explain what is obviously, I think, an inconsistency between the two positions.

Mr. Chairman, I will take this opportunity to reassure the hon. member immediately that when the formal note is ready it will be submitted to parliament. I have made that statement at least twice in this house, as has the Prime Minister, who has also given that assurance.
Regarding this interview to which reference has been made, let me say in the first place that I understand General Partridge was interviewed before he took over the command, before the integrated command was ever established. The second point is that the article was submitted to the R.C.A.F. for security clearance, because there was some references made in it to equipment which was then held by the R.C.A.F., and the United States authorities did not want to publish any information about Canadian equipment without getting clearance. But there was no question of the article being submitted to me; I never saw it until it appeared in print. Mr. Chairman, I am sure the minister noted the welcome the committee gave to his statement that any note finally agreed upon would be submitted to the house. He then said that he had made such a statement before. It was my recollection that he did not go that far, and perhaps it was for that reason that the committee was so glad to hear his categorical statement today. As a matter of fact, on a previous occasion when the estimates of the minister's department were being considered, on December 5, as recorded on page 1940 of Hansard, I put this question to the minister:
Is it fair to assume then, in view of the importance of that formal note between the two governments that it will be drawn in such terms- in other words, leaving out the elements of security -so that the note may be tabled here and also tabled in the appropriate place in the United States?
To which the minister replied:
I would hope that would be the case. I say I would hope, because naturally we are dealing with another government and we would have to get the consent of that government before tabling it. So I say I would hope it would be drawn up in such terms that there would be no doubt that it could be tabled.
Well, the minister has gone one step further today. If I understood him aright he said it would be tabled and that this house would
(Mr. Martin (Essex East).]

have it. I am sure we welcome that and I hope it will be in such a form that an appropriate motion will be presented to parliament and parliament will have the opportunity to decide for or against this joint defence arrangement. May I say to the minister that in making these arrangements we hope he will bear in mind that there is a difference between an arrangement which provides merely for reports to a body such as NATO and a command which draws its authority from a civilian authority such as NATO.
While I am on my feet may I just spell out briefly what I referred to earlier today by directing the minister's attention to sections 32 and 33 of the National Defence Act. These are the sections I had in mind when I was speaking earlier, under which the governor in council does have authority at any time to place any component, unit or person in the forces on active service. This can be done in Canada or abroad. It can be done by reason of an emergency for the defence of Canada or in consequence of any action undertaken by Canada under the United Nations charter, the North Atlantic treaty or any other similar instrument for collective defence that may be entered into by Canada. However, Mr. Chairman, the point of section 33 of the National Defence Act is that if the government does exercise this authority which it has of putting any Canadian personnel on active service, if parliament is not in session at the time parliament must be called within ten days of that action having been taken. I suppose it is a question of whether or not these personnel at Colorado Springs today are on active service. Does the minister want to comment on that?
All the regular forces of Canada are on active service. They have never been taken off active service since the Korean war.

But, Mr. Chairman, when they were placed on active service for the purpose of the Korean war, if my memory serves me right, the order in council specifically referred to the operations in Korea. From time to time as our service personnel have been placed on active service in Europe under NATO there have been orders in council directly relating to that service. My question is the obvious one. Has there been any order in council providing for these personnel to be on active service at Colorado Springs? If they are not on what is active service now, what would happen if under the direction of General Partridge or Air Marshal Slemon they were put on active service?

These things are routine. We all agree that these are things that may have to be done on the basis of a split-second decision but we urge the minister not to think of them as such routine military measures that he or the government forgets the parliamentary requirements as spelled out in the act under which the minister's department operates.

Mr. Chairman, I should like to say a few words on this at the present time. I believe this is one of the most important acts that has taken place within our Department of National Defence since the time of Korea. From the interest shown by the speakers thus far I think the importance of this subject has been demonstrated to the house and the concern which most of us feel is over the possible surrendering of our sovereign rights or of the civil authority becoming secondary to military authority.
I do not believe that any of us is opposed to co-operation or integration if you want to call it that but we are fearful that co-operation may mean a surrender of our sovereign rights. However I was glad to hear the minister inform us that nothing like this will take place. He assures us that the chiefs of the general staff are reporting directly to him. On the basis of that statement I would assume that he has some knowledge of the progress that is being made. If such is the case I am wondering why a little more of that knowledge is not given to the house.
I must say I have listened to this discussion quite carefully and I do not know a great deal more about this question than I did on December 5 when it was first raised in this house. Surely the minister must have knowledge of some progress that has been made. He must know something about what is going on. I believe it is up to him to report to this parliament whatever accomplishments have occurred.
There was one other statement made by the minister and I do not know if I correctly understood him. If that is the case I would like to know why a similar action has not taken place so far as Canada is concerned. If this has transpired I think it is a serious matter and something of which we should be made aware.
One other question I have concerns finance. I should like to know what arrangements have been made or are being contemplated for the sharing of the costs of the operation of NORAD?

Mr. Chairman, I have a question I should like to ask the minister. So far the discussion has been about what could be done in the event of enemy bombers coming over but I am interested in knowing what is the situation regarding enemy submarines. How near could they come to the coast of North America before we would be in a position to take action against those submarines? We have been informed that Russia has 500 submarines and in a short space of time will have 1,200. We have also been informed that they are armed with rocket-launching devices so I think most of us would believe that in the event of war Russia would probably use them for the purpose of launching atomic missiles against towns in the United States. At what distance could they be attacked by our planes if they were spotted?

There is nothing to prevent any vessel coming through the territorial waters which area in general is three miles out. They could not possibly be attacked unless they committed some overt act of war. If a Russian submarine attacked a Canadian vessel then appropriate action could be taken by any Canadian naval vessel or any Canadian aircraft which was in the vicinity but as for merely cruising up to the territorial waters of Canada there is nothing to prevent a vessel of another country doing so.

That is the point that concerns me. The leader of the C.C.F. mentioned the other day that he thought there was reason for Russia to be concerned due to the fact that she had been ringed around by bases of the western allies. Personally I think we are in a far more vulnerable position because we can be ringed around by a series of moving bases, looking upon these submarines as moving bases. I believe General Gruenther suggested that these submarines are equipped with rocket-launching devices and if this is so what is to prevent them at a certain specified time launching an attack on towns all around the American continent?
The minister says we could not take any action against them as long as they were cruising. Does that mean to say that if Russia did decide to make an attack upon this country she could send her submarine fleet out, put them at strategically located points around the continent, and at a given moment fire these rockets at targets on this continent and that we would not be in a position to take action against them until the rockets had been launched? It seems to me that we are in an extremely vulnerable position.

I will admit that we are in a vulnerable position and that is a threat which

National Defence we have to face but as long as there are naval craft of another country cruising off our shores in a peaceful way we certainly cannot take any hostile action against those craft. We are not going to start a war. If they start launching rockets against us then of course we will take immediate action against the submarines. Let me stress the fact that it is the fear of retaliation which we hope will stop the foolhardiness of any country in attacking this continent by any means whatever.

Can the minister tell us a little more about the status of the United States forces under General Partridge's command? As I recall it, he said a short while ago that General Partridge would have no authority whatever to commit the forces under his command to any action except that of defensive action of North America. Does that imply that the forces which the United States are placing under General Partridge and under Air Vice Marshal Slemon are to be under the complete control of a joint political group composed of the United States and Canada in the same way that the forces of NATO are under the NATO political organization, or would it be possible for the United States authority to decide that the forces under General Partridge were to be deployed in some such way as the hon. member for Algoma East suggested a few moments ago? Would that be possible because of the threat of an attack from the Chinese mainland forces on the communist government owing to some action they might have taken on Formosa? The point I want to get clear in my mind is this. Are the forces under this joint command going to be relinquished from purely national control and placed under the control of a political organization set up by Canada and the United States in the same way that NATO forces are under the NATO council?

General Partridge has operational control over the United States air forces allocated for the defence of the North American continent and operational control over the Canadian air forces allocated for the control of the North American continent. I sometimes wonder whether there is not some confusion amongst hon. members in believing that there is some relation between the strategic air command of the United States, which is a force of retaliation, and General Partridge's command. They are two entirely separate commands. General Partridge's command is purely a defence command of the North American continent. He has no offensive role whatsoever.
No-
No offensive role.

Mr. Chairman, it hinges, of course, on the definition that is given to the term "defensive". It might very well be that in the opinion of the strategists at the time the North American continent could only be defended in a certain instance by operations outside North America, and that is the point that we want to get clear and that, incidentally, is the point that this parliament should have clear and it would have it clear if this government had followed the normal procedure of presenting to this house a clearly outlined treaty which would outline and define the terms used. That has not been done, and so far we have only the suggestion of the minister that we shall have tabled in this house the notes which have been exchanged between the two governments. We do not know whether those notes are going to define clearly to us just what is considered to be defensive action, preventive action, if you like, for the defence of North America. I think we should have that clearly in our minds because otherwise we may find our forces involved in operations which the Canadian people and the Canadian parliament will not be prepared to consider as legitimate defensive action.
I understood the minister's announced policy to be that the reserve training such as weekend flying, air force training of reserve officer flyers, is to be discontinued. Is that correct?

No, that is not correct. Some time before this government came into power difficulties were experienced in fitting the role of the auxiliary forces of the R.C.A.F. into a fighter role. It was thought before the jet aircraft age came in that they could have been utilized to supplement the fighter squadrons of the R.C.A.F. Experience is showing that that cannot be done, and more emphasis is being placed on the role of search and rescue and on transport which is being allotted to the various auxiliary squadrons. It is not intended in any way to disband the auxiliary squadrons of the R.C.A.F., but there will be some change of role.
Has their flying time or their training time in that role been reduced?

I do not think there has been any reduction in training time but it may be that they will have to adjust their type of training to the new role. I would like to say that many of the auxiliary squadrons are doing extremely valuable work in connection with the "Pinetree" line. Personnel have gone there and are capable of relieving regular personnel for quite long periods, and that seems to be a very suitable role indeed for the auxiliary squadrons.

I mention this because I listened to the minister's reply this morning to the hon. member for Nanaimo about our dependence for the defence of Canada upon the United States air force. I notice that of late the United States forces, particularly the air force division, are advertising more and more the type of training that we give here. They are suggesting that retired airmen should take time at weekends to take this sort of training in the new planes. It is encouraging them. I wondered whether that would have any effect upon the minister's policy in Canada?
Will the minister do the same with this division of the service as he has done with the others and give us the figures of short spending for the years 1956 and 1957, and tell us whether the estimates are in line with his expenditures for the years 1957 and 1958?

This year the estimate was $784,173,000, of which it is now estimated $783,742,000 will be spent, which indicates an underexpenditure of $431,000 which is about as close estimating in both cases as I think it is humanly possible to get.
Can the minister also tell us something about the deferments or the cancellations of contracts in the two categories, one, the building construction program and the other, supply contracts?
Under acquisition and construction of buildings, acquisition of lands, etc., there is an estimated saving of $5 million.
Is this cancellation or deferment?
It includes both.
Can the minister apportion the $5 million between cancellation and deferment?
I do not have the figure broken down in those categories.
What about supplies?
With respect to aircraft, engines, and equipment there is a reduction of $20 million. A good deal of that has resulted from the cancellation of the Mark VI, CF-100.

Apparently the item we are now discussing is going to go through very shortly. I am sure there are very few men in public life who will get $2 million a day for seven days a week and 52 weeks in the year through parliament with as little trouble as the minister. Something over $784 million will

Mr. Chairman, I do not want to delay the estimates but before I go on to the subject I want to discuss may I say to the minister that I appreciate his co-operation very much in connection with the submarine menace about which I spoke some time ago in parliament. The minister has been most kind and co-operative and I should like him and the house to know that I appreciate his co-operation.
To get back to the command of the North American continent, I mentioned before that we in Newfoundland are in a rather different position from the rest of Canada in that we have United States forces stationed on our soil, including United States air force personnel in goodly numbers. We know that we are dependent on them very largely for our defence.
Having regard to the discussion so far and the information the minister has been kind enough to give us, I think there is a bit of confusion in the minds of some of us, certainly in my mind. I am not concerned now with the political aspect of the North American command although I agree that the military should be subservient to the civil. But I am not clear in my mind yet and I am afraid that we may have a second edition of Pearl Harbour. Those of us who have read the report of what happened there know that at that time the United States commander was in a state of uncertainty with respect to where his authority began and where it ended. The consequence was that he hesitated to take command and to set forces in motion to offset the raid by the Japanese aircraft.
I am afraid that unless the command difficulty is settled once and for all so that we will know who is to give orders without consultations with anybody we may find ourselves, particularly in Newfoundland, involved in a second Pearl Harbour. I am not


concerned who commands the air force, whether it is a United States general or a Canadian air marshal. We all agree that co-operation should exist from the highest to the lowest level if we are to have full co-ordination. I do not know yet whether General Partridge's appointment has been confirmed by the Canadian government or whether Air Marshal Slemon's appointment has been confirmed by the United States government, but I do know that the United States and Canada are in this thing together and we cannot be successful unless we have the fullest co-operation.
As I said a moment ago we have the United States air force in goodly numbers in Newfoundland. I want to be assured that General Partridge, or Air Marshal Slemon, whoever it may be, if an act of aggression is committed against our shores, either from submarines or from the air, will have full authority to take counter action immediately without any consultation whatever with this government or the United States government. I think that is necessary, that is vital if we are to have the protection which our people deserve. It is believed by military strategists and military tacticians that if an attack does come-God forbid that it should -it is going to come suddenly, without any warning. There will be no time for consultation with Ottawa or Washington. I trust that whoever is in command will have full authority to act immediately. Naturally he will have to tell the two governments what he has done, but whoever he may be he should have full authority to act immediately without any prior consultation.
I do ask the minister if he could, and if he would, assure me on this point. He has given me several answers before, but I do not think the answer is clear as to who has full authority to act at the moment. It may be that in this exchange of notes about which the minister has been speaking this afternoon, and which no doubt will be followed by a formal agreement between the two governments, this matter will be ironed out. But until that has happened, and until it is approved by both the United States and the Canadian government, I do believe these commanders should have that authority now. I do ask the minister if he has any comment to make upon it, and if he can give me that assurance.

I should like to assure the hon. member that the United States squadrons now based in Newfoundland are under the operation control of the Canadian air defence commander at St. Hubert, and that he has authority at once to engage, according to the accepted terms of engagement, any

hostile plane which is approaching Newfoundland, without reference any further because the terms of the agreement have already been accepted.

I should like to thank the minister for that explanation. It is information we have been trying to get for some time. If the arrangements are now made and that can happen I think that should satisfy our people. I thank him for the information.

I should like the minister to give us some details about item 22, page 344, concerning an expenditure of $1,754,000. I should like to ask him also whether in the case of the item for the air force this money was designated for the recreational branch of the Royal Canadian Air Force. An article written in the Ottawa Journal of Friday, October 25, suggests that the Royal Canadian Air Force recreational branch will receive a chop by national defence department.

The answer to the last question is that we recognize the importance of recreational facilities in the maintenance of morale of all the forces, perhaps particularly the R.C.A.F. in these northern stations where there are not the usual means for recreation. For instance, on the "Pinetree" line there are bowling alleys established at the stations. In some cases they have swimming pools, and every reasonable facility is given for recreation.
In so far as the question about the other items which appear at the bottom of page 344 is concerned, they cover the same sort of items as were covered by the other items for the army, such as laundry, grants to the band, physical fitness equipment and so on. There is an amount there of $127,000, giving an indication of the extent to which we are encouraging recreation. I notice that it is expected that amount will be overspent by $16,400 compared to 1956-57, which would certainly give an indication that we are encouraging recreation. There is another item for entertainment expenses. As I have already pointed out, in these northern areas we believe it is important to encourage that sort of thing. Mr. Chairman, all members realize the estimates we are discussing are very large indeed. I imagine that no matter what the point of view we would hope these estimates in the future might be reduced. I am rather disturbed about a report in this evening's Ottawa Journal, a statement said to have been made by the parliamentary assistant to the Minister of National Defence, the hon. member for Edmonton West. I think the committee is entitled to know whether in making this statement he is in fact stating government policy or what government policy is likely to be. This is a Canadian Press dispatch from Calgary, dated January 4, and it reads:
The parliamentary assistant to Defence Minister Pearkes said last night Canada may have to increase its defence expenditures beyond the 1957 budget of $1,750,000,000.
He is talking about the major changes that may be forthcoming, and he goes on to say, and this is in quotation marks:
"Today it is tremendous; tomorrow it may even be greater. We are going to face increased responsibilities and must reorientate our thoughts."
In plain English that would suggest to me that the parliamentary assistant is saying that we are going to be asked to pass larger estimates for national defence in the coming fiscal year. I hope that the Minister of National Defence may be able to say that the expression of his parliamentary assistant is not correct as reported in the newspaper. We know that sometimes the reports in the press are not wholly accurate. I hope he is able to assure the committee that, when the estimates are brought down for the new

Supply-National Defence fiscal year in the matter of a short time they will not in fact contain substantial increases. We in this group feel that the estimates for national defence in the future should be reduced and that there are other ways by which the government can spend money to provide defence in a more secure manner than by continuing to spend the very large sum of $lf billion as a rather fixed amount for an indefinite period.
I think it would be an act of faith on the part of Canada if, in the coming fiscal year, we reduced the amount of money we are voting for national defence and used the resources of this country in other ways to assist people in underdeveloped countries and so on. However, I think the committee has a right to know whether or not the parliamentary assistant in fact is stating the government policy when he says that Canada may have to increase its defence expenditure in the coming year and then spells this statement out by referring to the increased responsibilities and so on.

I have not seen the article in question nor have I heard the remarks made by my parliamentary assistant who, I believe, is in Alberta today. Furthermore, as I stated earlier in this discussion, I cannot discuss next year's estimates while we are still considering the estimates of 1957.

With great respect to the minister, may I say that I do not think the statement that he has now made is an adequate one. Surely, in discussing the defence estimates for any given fiscal year, it is fair to ask what the government's continuing policy in this field is going to be. With the new fiscal year coming along in less than three months and with his parliamentary assistant being credited with making statements of government policy outside the house, I think the committee has a right to know whether those statements, as attributed to him in the press, are a correct statement of government policy. Of course the minister was not there. I am not asking the minister to say whether or not the parliamentary assistant in fact made those statements. But surely, when they appear in the press, it is fair to ask whether the statements as reported in the press are in fact a statement of the minister's own position and that of the government.
Shall the Royal Canadian Air Force item carry?

Since the minister is not talking on this question we will have a chance to find out in the future whether the parliamentary assistant has been more appropriately speaking for the government at the political convention in Calgary than has the

minister himself. I want to refer to another question. The matter of whether the continuing policy to produce substantial quantities of CF-105's is a correct one is, of course, rather controversial. But I should like to know from the minister what amount of money has already been spent in the development of the CF-105 and what commitment the government has made by way of policy that will result in future expenditures for the development of the CF-105.

The CF-105 is being developed as a supersonic interceptor. The start was made on this aircraft some few years ago and this year we decided to continue for one year or more the development of this aircraft. We are not committed any further than to continue the development for another year, with the right even then of discontinuing that development should the circumstances warrant taking such a step. I am told that the total amount spent so far on the development of this aircraft is $89,000,641.
Over what period of time?
This is up to the end of October, 1957 from the time when the initial research work started, which was two or three years ago.

I wonder whether the
minister could indicate what will be the total cost by the time it is off the line?

It will depend entirely on the number of aircraft, if any, which are ordered. I will frankly admit there is a very heavy expenditure in developing this particular type of aircraft. The demand at the present time is not large, as no other country is at present ordering this aircraft. We must develop it for ourselves, and the expense is heavy.
Can the minister say when the one-year period ends for which the development has been continued?

I think it was the first of
October of this year.
Can the minister say what are the likely expenses that will be incurred during this further one-year period? The expense has been some $89 million up to now.

The whole situation will
have to be reviewed in the light of the threat that there is of manned bombers. This is an aircraft designed to meet manned bombers. We know that Russia has considerable numbers of manned bombers capable of flying over this country. While the manned bomber, flying at great heights and

at great speeds, is in the armament of a possible enemy, we must keep aircraft which are capable of meeting that threat. But as the bomber threat may decrease and the missile threat may become more definite the whole situation has to be reviewed. One of the difficulties is that we are not looking at the situation which will occur just a year hence, we must try to pierce the future for five years hence.

The minister has already
informed the committee that the cost of development up to October 1, 1957, was some $89 million and that the program is being continued for another period of 12 months. Is the minister able to estimate the cost of continuing the program for the one-year period which I take it is from October 1, 1957 to October 1, 1958?
No, I have not a detailed estimate of that cost at all.

I think the minister's
predecessor was able to give us some estimate a year ago. It is hard to understand why the minister now is not able to give the committee at least as much information as his predecessor gave. Surely before embarking on a program of this sort the government would want to have some idea as to what the target was going to be. Surely the minister can say something more than that the government has spent $89 million up to October of this year. Can the minister not say what the estimated cost to the treasury will be of completing the job undertaken?
The figures for next year will be included in next year's estimates.

But, Mr. Chairman, a year ago the minister's predecessor was able to give the committee some information. I have not got the figures before me, but it is hard to understand why the present minister is not able to give us as much information as we were able to have a year ago regarding what the total cost was going to be. I think he could bring this estimate up to date if he wishes to co-operate with the committee.

Up to November 30 the money which has already been spent on air frame development amounted to $11,038,376; on the Iroquois engine development, $7,951,487; and on the electronic development, $4,355,480. That is the total development for the year, $23,345,343.

That is helpful. The minister has the information up to the end of November. Surely he could make a forecast for the balance of the year. If this amount has been increased by $20 million for this
Supply-National Defence period, surely some estimate has been made as to what will be the total amount involved for the rest of the 12-month period. Could the minister not give us that information?

Can the minister inform the committee how many CF-105 planes the department expects to have in the air at the end of this further continuing period of development? The minister may recall that last year his colleague the Minister of Transport announced that a new marine agency vessel under construction for the Prince Rupert agency was being fitted with a helicopter landing deck. I wonder if there will be a helicopter under the jurisdiction of the


Department of Transport attached to that vessel? Is this helicopter landing deck being provided for use by the search and rescue unit.

There is one other matter in connection with the search and rescue situation which I would like to put before the committee before this item carries. As the minister will recall, he and I have had some discussion about the situation with reference to the R.C.A.F. establishment at Tofino. The idea of the need for units of search and rescue on the west coast of Vancouver island is not really a new one. The area originally covered by the radio at Tofino is now covered by two larger stations, one at Holberg on the north of Vancouver island and the other in the state of Washington which made the necessity of maintaining the station at Tofino for defence purposes unnecessary, but Tofino airport is being transferred to the Department of Transport and I believe they will be making arrangements for the maintenance of that field in a rather less active state than has been the case in the past.
I take it from what the minister said that the matter of the maintenance of this radio beacon is something that could be properly taken up with the Department of Transport?
That would be maintained, if maintained, by the Department of Transport.
